WORKING MEN AND THEIR LEADERS.
THE Daily News of Monday, the 13th,
contains a long paragraph purporting to be
an account of a meeting of Carpenters and
Joiners' delegates, at the Brown Bear tavern,
Bloomsbury, for the purpose of arranging the
preliminaries of the large public meeting
which took place on the Tuesday night follow-
ing, in St. James's Hall. At [that meeting
the names of three gentlemen, well-known as
old leaders in the society were proposed as
speakers, and rejected by those assembled "on
the ground that they were not now working
as carpenters, and that it was desirable to
show the employers that the men engaged in
the trade were quite competent to conduct
their own movement without the extraneous
aid of parties whose advocacy might be more
damaging than otherwise from their promi-
nence in agitation."
Those words are quoted verbatim et literatini,
from the journal named, but before offering
any comment upon them it may not be amiss
to point out that they have since formed the
substance of a paragraph which has made its
appearance in many of the leading provincial
journals, particularly those published in the
manufacturing districts, where trades unions
have been troublesome to employers, and
whore, naturally enough, the names of the men
who are prominent actors in them are very
distasteful to the manufacturing and shop-
keeping classes.
Passing this by as digression—it will be in
place to say here that the right of the various
trades societies to conduct their own business
in their own way is not in dispute. Nor does
what is said apply to the Carpenters and
Joiners exclusively. It is the poliey of the
proceeding which is called in question, a
policy which other trades may adopt, and
which, if true and sound, they ought to apply,
in practice as soon as possible. But which,
if neither true nor sound, if on the contrary,
most ,unsound, and therefore dangerous to the
bestinterests of trades associations, should be
repudiated at once universally and indignantly
—it is right here to glance at what this policy

involves.
Nothing need be said of men who, through
a variety of causes, have left the workshop,
but who keep up some kind of connection
with the old craft, and who respect their old
shopmates. These men were not pointed at
by the resolution referred to. The men
touched by this resolution are those who have
held official positions, or who have taken an
active lead. in strikes ; who, in fact, are marked
men, because of their activity on the side of

are of high reputation, good faculty, long ex-
perience, who have done in the past, and are
capable of doing in the present, good service
to their fellows. They are capable of
thoroughly understanding and clearly explain-
ing to the public, and even to the men them-
selves, such matters as may come into dispute
between working men and their employers.
This may not be due to any mEntal superiority
over other men who arc actually at work at
the trade, but rather the result of special
experiences and special studies, which, how-
era induced, have certainly given them
the capability of advising and directing;
a capability which has as a rule been exor-
cised with great prudence and discretion. Let
personal prejudice say what it may of such
men as are or have been secretaries of
trades unions, it is impossible for those who
know them not to admire the ability, the zeal
and the honesty with which they devote them-
selves to their duties. And that man indeed
must be either utterly blind. to facts, or utterly
opposed. to the spirit and practice of trades
unionism, who would deny or in any way dis-
parage their services.
"Why, then, it may be asked, should such

len be declared unfit to take part in the

business of their several trades ? They have,
it is said, teased to work at the trade. Yes,
many of them have, because they have had to
work for the trade in a seorotarial or some other
capacity, which in a few years necessarily
renders them unfit for the workshop. Others
have been driven out by employers as a
punishment for their activity at some critical
juncture. Bat, however they may have left
the workshops, if they possess intelligence,
devotion to the cause, and general fitness
of character, surely it is the merest
"midsummer madness" to refuse their advice
and assistance because they have ceased to
work at their several trades.

The carpenters and joiners gave another reason

—"they wish to show their employers that. the
men engaged in the trade can conduct their
own movement." There is no doubt in the
world the employers will be delighted to see
this, and will openly declare it to be a very
wise act, though secretly they will think of it
as something quite different. But, why do
the men want to convince the masters of this?
Why do they want to convince anybody of it?
Canit raise men in anybodies' estimation to say
they have cut off a hand or plucked out an eye?
Should they not rather seek to convince their
employers that they are determined to utilise
every available element of strength in the
contest they are about to enter on? Should they
not rather have tried to convince them that
they were united to a man, that the young and
the old stand together, the worker and the
non-worker, the man of veteran experience
and the young zealous soldier, that every well-
wisher of the old craft had. sunk all differences
so that they might unite all strengths for the
good of their common cause. It is very
much to be desired that the men may be
able to fight their battle alone, but even though
they should it is neither modest, nor grateful
to repudiate, as matter of duty, the services of
those men who have hitherto been regarded as
their best and most useful friends.

Bad as this is, however, it may be truly
said. that worse remains behind. Another
reason for repudiating their old friends was
lest they " might damage their CAII2O throuksh.

their prominence in agitation." Damage their
cause where? In whose eyes? Damage their
cause how? What can this superlative
stupidity mean? Under what temporary
alienation of understanding can working men
be brought to utter such nonsense? Can it be
believed possible that men in t:he management
of trades unions regard it as damaging, that
their leading members should take part in
public action on questions of general interest
*their class? and practically lay down the
rule that to seek to better their fellows in any
way but by trades' unionism is a disqualifying
offence in the eyes of their brother members?
We could understand the matter if any
member of a trades' society dragged political,
religious, or disputed social questions into
their meetings so as to interfere with the pro-
gress of their proper business. Such an
evident impropriety ought to be stringently
provided against. This is not what the
carpenters and joiners did. They raised the
common enemies' cry of "agitator." They
made the work done in their interest a re-
proach against those who did it, and gave
them punishment for payment. Those who

have laboured for the extension of popular
liberty, for the promotion of public education,
for an increase of social comfort amongst the
people, have always been called "agitators,"
by men who are opposed to popular progress.
They have had to take the abuse and loss and
pain from the hands of the exalted and power-

'ul ; but this is a matter of course, and there-

fore to he expected. But when those for
whom the ill-rewarded up-hill light is under-
taken, strike also, and join in the cry, "away
with them—away with them," the deep in-
gratitude of such a proceeding adds every-
thing that can be added of baseness and
turpitude.

Besides, it may be asked whether there is in
the whole circle of human folly, wide as that
is, a more singular example of self-stultifica-
tion? After many long years of political and
social degradation, after a fight carried, on
rather through hope in the future than any
expectation of immediate results, the, people
have gained possession of political 'power,
by which they may obtain for themselves and
their children blessings unknown to past
generations of working men. We are told
that to agitate, to stimulate by speech and
thought—to urge by exathple, that the future
shall be entered on by 'working Men, and
their new power made instrumental in the
production of new blessings to themselves and
to the nation—is a work damaging to the ,
character of a working man and ruinous to his
reputation—is simply an insult to the common
'sense of the community. Now the field is
ready—now that the harvest over-ripe demands
the sickle that it may be gathered and turned
to use, now that there is a chance of pro-
curing for poor men's children an education
fitting them for manly independence and true
usefulness in life, now that working men may
obtain that position from which they can pro-
mote all their honest interests by firmly
rooting national law deep in the soil of justice
and right strange to say, at this most
auspicious moment the voices of working men
reach our ears, demagading, under pains and
penalties, silence and inactivity, striking
their best friends with fear and despondency,
when they ought to be cheering and
encouraging them in their good work.

It cauaot bo bdieved that what is bur°

combated prevails to any extent among
working men as settled conviction. It is
difficult to credit that those who uttered the
language reported can seriously, after reflec-
tion, think themselves right. It may have
been some personal objection which led to the
laying down of such a policy; but personal
objections should never be made a pretext for
stating or enforcing vicious principles. To
fight the battle which lies before them as an
inevitable duty, the working men must carry
with them their whole strength. They must
not refuse this battle on any legitimate ground
—political, social, or industrial. They must
not, by accepting the slanderous sophisms of
their enemies, condemn themselves to im-
potency and sterility. They should all be
"agitators," each in his own way, each doing
what he can best do to aid in obtaining the
victory. England in her higher life belongs
to Englishmen, not to any of its classes. It
is the duty of all to love and serve her, and of
none more than working men. They cannot
confer honours on their leaders, they never
have overburdened them with pecuniary re-
wards; but they may give them loyalty
and gratitude, if for no other reason for the
selfish one of encouraging others to follow
them to the front that the cause of labour may
ultimately triumph, even through the sacri-
floe of these men.

THE GREAT DISCOVERY.
ME truth which is verified in the know-
ledge of the causes of Evil and of Good to man
has long been known as a general truth by
many philosophers. But by the world in
general it has not been known, and has been
denied. And merely to know it as a general
truth is comparatively unimportant. It itt not
merely the knowledge that there are causes
of Evil and of Good which is needed, it is the
knowledge of the causes themselves, and of
their influences in producing Evil and Good.
Men have had a general instinctive idea that
there are causes of Evil and of Good upon ,
which the char aoter and conduct of individuals
are more or less dependent, and have vaguely
endeavoured to substitute causes of Good for
causes of Evil. But not knowing the effects
of causes upon man, and not knowing where
the causation of the evil begins, they have
endeavoured to get .rid of the Evil while the
primary or root cause of it has remained
unsuspected in constant operation. They
have known that unkindness, untruthfulness,
injustice, &e., are unfavourable to man's
happiness are causes of Evil. But they
have not known the primary causes which
produce them, and, therefore, all the means
which they have employed to prevent or
remove these secondary causes of Evil have
been unsuccessful. For ages past they have
tried advice and exhortation, religious forms
and ceremonies, appeals to man's fears, and to
his hopes, and to his higher nature, rules of
duty and commandments, threats and pro-
mises, blame and praise, punishments and
rewards, and endless legal enactments. How
unsuccessful all these means of education
and social government have hem as influences
to cause men to be invariably kind to each
other, and truthful, and just—to do to others
in all things as they would have others to do
to them—every one may fsee on all idea.

And why have they been failures? Because
they have left the root-cause of Evil in full
operation ; and because ithey: have been
dictated in part by the ignorance and the
erroneous ideas which are the root-cause of
Evil; and because the commands, and threats,-.
and blame, and punishment have therefore
been employed in an unjust spirit of unkind-
ness and harshness—a spirit which is the
effect of the root-cause of Evil, and which can
never be a cause of kindness, and mutual
love; taq trpthfulness, and justice.

in fact, that man can do can be effectual in
education or in social government while the

and in unceasing operation within him, onus-

in iy: Tqpeat that the ascertaining of 'these

ileent of all the discoveries which man .has had
to make in his progress from his -primitive
ignorant cud barbarous condition to the high

44 man now knows, and all that ,he is able to

lectual and moral development is so defective

Mr. OWEN tells us that early in life, before ho

observing, in himself and in others, the facts
which it suggested to him, to perceive that
the individuals of all nations and peoples are
the results, in their charaoter and conduct, of
the causes or conditions by which they are in-

Iluenced, in the language, ideas, feelings, and
general proceedings, of, the persons by whom
they arc. Surrounded, and iii the 'Various ma-
terial objects by which they are affected-the
general results being similar, but the effects
iii individuals being to some extent varied, in

tion (the effects of conditions external to the
individual, and preceding his birth), and partly
peeuliaritiei in the external conditions, in

ate influenced from birth. So far he was
right. But in this there was no now dis-

inferenees (also by no means new),-which be

inference, Which does.! follow from the pre-

of the subject, and which is a fundamental

tive inference which does not follow from the

premisses, which is no in agreement with the
facts, and Which is a fundamental error ex-
tremely injurious in its effects—the denial of

stitution. The first inference is, that man is
the creature of causation—that there is always
a cause, or there are always causes, constitu-
tional and external, of Which the character,
opinions, and determinations of the individual
are the effects. This is the assertion of the

the !Thii.versality of Law. The other infer-
ence,' which was confounded with this by

and determinations of the individual are in
all cases formed for him and not by him. In
th s inference a highly important truth is
denied—namely, that man is mentally an
agent in the fortniug of his character, &o.;
or that ho acquires, in the progress of his
intellectual and moral development, a power
of self-government, subject, of course, to the
laws of causation. To be . correct, therefore,
the truth relative to causation should be quell-.

tied by being cainbined with the truth rela-
tive to man's mental power, instead of being
exaggerated by being combined with the
denial of this truth. Our inference' should
be, that although man's character, opinions,
and determinations are the effects of the. in-
fluences or causes to which his peculiar con-
stitution is subjected from birth, they are
effects which he is himself to soma- extent•an
agent in producing, under causation; or, that
although man is an agent mentally, or ex-

He tells us that by observing the facts of

He felt greatly surprised that men had. re-
mained so long in ignorance f the causes of
evil and of good—that they had never success-
fully investigated to their .practical com-
mencement the facts In -which the effects of
causew in the forming of character, and in the
producing of evil and of good to man in other
respects, are. manifested. And he set to work
to investigate these causes to their source, by
carefully tracing, in himself and others,'
the effects of influences of various, kinds
upon the feelings .and conduct, and upon
the formation of character. Ha found that
his own feelings were powerfully influenced
for good by the knowledge of the truth
that man is the creature of pausation—
that when he considered the causes of the
injurious feelings and conduct, and of the
defective character of individuals, he was
caused, by the ideas of these causes, to have
feelings of charity, and kindness, and pity,
for those who had been so unfavourably in-
fluenced as to have been caused to acquire
injurious qualitios, and to: think, and feel, and
act injuriously. And be found that his feel- '
ings were so powerfully influenced by those
considerations, that he ceased to be angry and
irascible as others were. By these ideas the
social and sympathetic tendencies of human
nature were enlightened and powerfully excited
within him, and his sentiment of justice was
enlightened, and he was caused to desire to
promote, as far as ho was able, the happiness
of his fellow-beings; to be strongly influenced
to do to others in all things as he would have
others. to do to him. Ho thus found the root-
cause of good in this fundamental idea, and
in the knowledge of causes.
On the other hand, he found that the unkind
and angry feelings, and the easily-excited
irascibility, in endlessly varied forms and
degrees, now so conspicuous in all characters,
are the elects of the idea than man is himself
the primary cause of his qualities, opinions,
feelings, and acts; that is, of ignorance, and
the denial of the truth relative to causation
and of ignorance of the pauses of evil and o
good. He found that, while man is under the'
influence of this ignorant and erroneous idea
(an idea which the young are now caused to
acquire instinctively through the examples,
the looks, and words, and acts of the persons
by whom they are influenced from birth), his
natural and most useful tendency to repel
what is painful and injurious to him is excited
into over-activity, by the qualities and acts of
individuals which arc displeasing to him; and
ho is thus caused to be irritable, irascible,
harsh, spiteful, quarrelsome, vindictive, and,
therefore, to manifest these feelings' in his
conduct, and to acquire a.character in which
they are always ready to be roused into activity.
And he found that, while man is thus morally
deteriorated by the influence of this false idea

—this,ignoAnce and denial of the Universality
of Law—he is kept by it intellectually in
ignorance and error upon this most important
subject. He scarcely thinks at all of the
.
causes of man's qualities, and feelings, and
acts, except blindly to attribute these Teets
to the individual himself as the primary ca.use
of them—that is, as producing them in him-
self by soma kind of mental agency which he
himself originates. And, of course, he never
can think of tracing out in himself and others
the facts in which the primary cause of evil
to be observed in constant operation. And
thus, so far as his influence extends, he be-
comes in this respect a cause of evil to others,
communicating to them, in their ignorance of

free-will) that man is himself the originating
or primary cause of his qualities, opinions,
and determinations. But I must reserve the
conclusion for another paper.

HENRY TUNIS.

THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACTS.

I TRUST you will allow me to answer the
letter of Mrs. JOSEPHINE BUTLER? Her
labours of love are, after all, but hers and
those of her few friends—and all honour be
to them—but, surely, these are very excep-
tional, and we all know that the cruelty of
women (especially ladies) has driven many
poor women to prositution, and is doing so
daily. The stern, cold, unforgiving nature of
their treatment of those frail ones who fall from
the ranks of respeotability, imposes an all but
impassible barrier to a return to the paths of
virtue. The dreary lives, too, led by many
domestic servants, the unnatural rules against
any intercourse with sweethearts, causing
clandestine, and, therefore, dangerous inter-
course, tend to the ruin of young women, and
there are numerous women who denounce
these sanitary laws, and who yet are, by their
cruelty, adding to the ranks of prostitution.
To allege, in answer to all this, that Mrs
JosEPaL BIITER and a few other ladies are
tender-hearted, benevolent, and merciful, even
to the fallen and degraded, does not in the
least disprove risy • assertions, which are, after
all, but truisms; nor does it change the
unreality, I had almost said, hypocrisy of
their loud cries against "instrumental viola-
tion," accompanied by the admission that if
the modesty of every woman were secure,
still the Acts would be objected. to.
Many ladies have taken offence, too, at my
charge of "ignorance." Now, I happen to
know that some of the most zealous opponents
of these laws are young unmarried ladies
under twenty-five. I venture to assert that
ignorance on these subjects is infinitely more
becoming to them thau the knowledge of an
ACTON or a PA.GET.

Your correspondent, Mr. JAMES STUART,
M.A., endeavours to prove that the poor are
unjustly treated in the working of these Acts
in favour of the rich. Now, if anyone is
interested in the question of health, it is the
poor man. The wealthy man may be diseased,
and he repairs at once to the best advice, he
avoids exposure to toil and bad weather, be
may even change his climate and seek health
on the shores of the Mediterranean, and the
disease may leave no permanently bad effects
on his constitution, or, at the worst, the

_
wealthy, invalid may find life very endurable
surrounded by every possible appliance of
luxury. But with the poor man all this is
changed. Compelled by necessity to toil in
the bad air of a crowded workshop, he keeps
his place in misery and. weariness, or he
labours in the cold, wet streets; his tissues full
of mercury, until his remedy may be even worse
than the disease; and so he dies, or he lives a
maimed, wretched life, and begets children
weak, and. fit only/or beggary and the work-
.house.

I know of no question of more importance,
to the working classes especially, than this.
Mr. CHRISTOPIIER NEVILE objects to see the
virtuous taxed on behalf of the vicious.
Well, put the question simply as one of

economy, eliminate all humanity from it, and
then, I assert, if you virtuous people won't,
pay to prevent vicious people from poisoning
the community, they will have to pay ten
times the amount in keeping alive the poor
dregs of humanity who are the offspring of
diseased parents. And I would say to you
moralists, that morals do not, and cannot,
flourish amidst weakly, and, therefore, povertt.
stricken and debased humanity.

Every advance in social and sanitary scienos
sh6jja us :mord anct mire how èar payipg
for preventible evils. Some great men de-
nounce excess of population. 'Without giving
any opinion on that vexed question, I am cer-
tain that we have an 'excess of a weakly popu-
lation, whose nnrvous systems are not equal
to the battle of life, and who are a grievous
burden on our resources. Aloohol, syphilis)
and such like poisons, are the cause of more
lunacy, crime, and misery, than many good
people are aware of, and flits reproach we bear
of putting "health before morals" savours or
zeal based on ignorance.

In the army and navy we have organized I
bodies of healthy men most valuable for saiii"
tory statistics. Scientific observers have given
us the most valuable but appalling statistios
on the direct injuries inflicted on these men ;
by the disease in question. Could civil society
be organised and observed in like manner, far
stronger proofs of direct and indirect injuries
might be furnished.

Mr. JAMES STUART indignantly denies that
prostitution is a necessity. That question is
beside the mark, we are not concerned with it;
but I would ask Mr. STUIRT if prostitution be
not a fact. Will he deny that it is as ancient
as history, and that no laws, civil or religious,
have ever suppressed it. Our simple duty is
to deal with the disease connected with it.
Let us take examples from Mrs. BUTLER'S
good deeds. She avows having assisted in the
care of
,prostitutes and sinners, of this disease.
Now did she not thereby incur the stupid
charge of encouraging these sinners ?• Had
she ,allowed her fallen friends to perish of
their disease, and, moreover, to. spread it,
would she not thereby have discouraged in-
continence, and even punished it? "But," it
will be answered, "she gave them religion and
pious counsel as well as medicines and nurs.
ing." . True, and this is what Government
provides for also, and sundry women have
been cleansed morally as well as physically
through these humane laws. To be consistent,
our opponents should object to any remedies
being applied to venereal diseases, and many
do. How true it is that the iwitinots of real
good women are right, though their logic fails.
Here we have Mrs. BUTLER sucoouring and.
healing poor wretched fallen women,- and
thereby incurring the reproaches so freely -
hurled at us of encouraging such creatures,
though she is indignant at Government doing
the same thing coercively. After all, govern-.
ment represents the aggregate of individuals.
If individuals pursue the hamane course of
Mrs. RIMER, why may we not all do it by
deputing Government to act for us, and as
prevention is better than cure, why net make
o certain trade give up its poison, under Co-
ercion, if not otherwise, before the infection
spreads'?

Lastly, lot me remark on the personal part
of this controversy. I have asserted, and I
reassert that the greater part of the ladies
who denounce these acts, spurn the poor frail
ones with inhuman contempt. Mrs. BUIL=
takes this as aimed at her personally. I sin-
cerely regret having given her this idea, for I
have long had a profound admiration for the
character of that excellent lady. Now, I
really think it would be as reasonable in me
to take as aimed at myself personally, her
remark that she "knows the secret lives of
gentlemen who patronize this class." As I ara•
not a patron of this class this remark does
not reach me, and as Mrs. BUTLER is not one
of those who spurn the fallen women, ray re-
marks ought not to have offended her.
HU3IPILRIC SANDWITIT.
