articles.text:
MEN AND WOMEN Ot TOIL.

ON the eve of the late outbreak, a Jamaican
overheard a black man, dilating on the wrongs
of his race, say, "Look, my friend, look at
de black man in this island of Jamaica and

look at de white man. De white man, he
governor, he judge, he planter, he master.
And de black man, what is be? De scum of
de eart. He sweat de brow and get nothing;
he offered plenty good advice how to conduct
herself in the station that Providence give

him," &c., &0..
~ The speaker, doubtless , felt, though not
understanding the cause, that it was a crying
injustice that his fellow-men ehould sweat de
brow and obtain a pittance only, whilst
the governor, judge; planter, p.nd master,
undergoing nothing like the same bodily
exhaustion in the performance of their duties,
should revel in the midst of pomp and luxury.
May not the labourers and artificers of this
country, slaveswhose services are appropriated,
though the. bodies are not, regard their rela-
tion to those set over them much in the same
light? Taking instances only of those who
truly do
,work, the new Somerton-GENERAL
for his official duties obligingly accepts six
thousand pounds a year, leaving out Sundays
only, about four hundred shillings a day,
whether employed or not; the judge who
presided at the TICUBOILNE trial receives seven
thousand pounds a year, excluding Sundays
and holidays, about six hundred shillings a
day. Only on occasions when sitting for some
time in his court in a vitiated air, a prevent-
able cause, does ho experience the bodily
exhaustion of the every day labourer who
gets but two shillings a day. " Tut," says
old FOGY, "look at the difference in value of
the services." Their value may be different,
Mr. FOGY, but payment for services according
to their value, in other words, according to the
necessities of those in want of them, leads to
extortion, as we have seen it would in the
ease of the two persons on the desert island;
it is the cause of the present cannibalism,
which can no longer be tolerated; man cannot
continue to oat up man. Were the Cervices of
the labour paid for according to the cost
principle, according to what the work of each
respectively cost in disagreeableness and bodily
exhaustion, the repugnance overcome, the
labourer, instead of being so iniquitously
underpaid, would frequently be more highly
remunerated than the judge.

_
"Oh ! I have you," again contends Mr.
FOGY. "There are few capable of filling the
office of a judge, so such a one can impose his
terms and. we must accede to them, but if one
bread-aud-butter producer will not work for
two shillings a day, there are hundreds eager
to take his place." That argument, Mr.
FOGY, has received some checks, and, ere
long, will be mated. • Intellectual superiority
does not justify extortion, no more than
physical . superiority did of yore. Mr.
MUSCLES, bread-and butter producer, has every
respect for Mr. BRAINS., He intends, however,
no longer to be his slave; he will work for and.
with biru on equal terms, on no other. If Ur.,
BRAINS agrees to this, well and good. ; if not,
Mr. MUSCLES will let him flourish as best he
can, he will no longer furnish him bread-and-
butter.

_
Men and women of toil! ho no longer the
mere instruments to produce wealth of the
political economists, and concern not yourselves
about Monarchy, republicanism, priests,
and their mythologies; or the House of Lords
or Commons. They will all disappear like a
dissolving view at the rate, and as soon as
your rights of labour, burden for burden,
comes to the fore. Regarding .it as a most
holy Strife, commence in real earnest the battle
of labour. Rise in your great might ; unfurl
the banner—industrial justice—and rally
round it.

St.rike one, strike all, and hard until
Your cause prevail, as soon it will..
It is your right,
And for it will tight.
And have it; yes, by God you will.

To marshal your forces and to know who will
enrol himself in the contest, let nature's
nobility, the noble and wise among you, men
and women, take counsel together and appor-
tion each city, town, village, and district of
each county into such portions and sub-
portions, that by opening offices of demand
and supply in each, the want of every indivi-
dual in the community may become known,
and every required statistic of the locality be
accurately obtained. Divide, divide, divide,
individualise. Have your ministers of land,

marine, fuel, food, and clothing, co.; caoh of
whom, adopted by acclamation, or self-elected
and approved of, -would individually be respon.
Bible for the proper and harmonious working
of his department. The minister of land
would proceed at once to inform himself all
about the houses and lands in his district,
which of the proprietors would agree to equity,
and which would not ; what the waste lands
and their nature, and what the best purposes
to put them to. The ministers of food would
ascertain the quantity of the various foods re-
quired and. the best source of supply. The
ministers of clothing the same. The fish
minister, the resources in his neighbourhood,
and the best mode of increasing the sea and
inland fisheries. The minister of marine
would look after the transport service and the
interest of the sailors, and so on. _ .

For a standard, or standards of cost, seleot
in your localities some staple specie of labour,
either of agriculture and manufacture, wheat,
cotton, or woollen goods-producing, with
which to compare other labour. The most
appropriate qualities for such a standard are
those which arc most invariable in quality,
most uniform in the amount produced by the
same amount of labour, and most .uniform in
the extent of the demand. One or more of
these being settled upon every individual,
might send an estimate of the rate compared
with any standard ho would furnish his labour.
An average might then be struck at which
most would be willing to work. Still, every
individual must be at liberty to deal in the
way ho thinks most conducive to his avian
interests.

In the transition from the present savageism
to harmonic relations, to guard against im-
position with respect to labour-notes, one
person only in each locality should issue
blank forms, so that every one by reference to
him could at once know the standing of each
one employing labour-notes. Those that
could not obtain credit for a circulating me-
dium would have to content themselves with
certifi•mtes of deposit of stored-up labour
from the storekeeper.

The present profit-making, getting some-

thing for. nothing system, offering the tempta-
tion of illicit gains and rapid wealth at the
expense of others, creates trade where there
is no necessity for it. On the cost principle,
exchanging will be reduced to the simplest
and most direct methods. Sonic large stores
will contain only one description of goods, and
other different kinds, each kind probably
superintended. on individual responsibility,

like stalls at a bazaar. This will close most
of the present shops, but they will serve as
barracks whilst building yourselves palatial
residences, where the economies of the large
scale will be observed, such as public dining,
reading, and billiard rooms, nursery, laundry,
Btc. Hotels at New York can accommodate
the population that would here form a large
village; and in them perfect retirement can be
enjoyed as well as all requisite companionship.
In the absence of the palatial residences, to
save labour and to make the most of your
resources, institute at once your public stores,
eating-houses, and other arrangements of the
largo wale. Cost price, at first, would be
composed of two elements—cost price in money
and cost price of the extra labour in buying,
selling, and delivering. In the country you
would likely establish your tents and military
ovens, and, employing the best cooks, use the
best and cheapest flesh-forming and heat-
forming goods, suoh as wheat, the legumes,
peas, beaus, &e., making what arrangement
you can with your brothers of the sea for all
the fish they can supply.
For clothing, devise a most simple form of
suitable material, and of the cheapest descrip-
ticn ; a 'uniform would not be at all objection-
able during the struggle, and let machinery
rattle away day and night, worked by
six-hour gangs, till everyone is comfortably
clothed.
All business matters should be conducted so
as to admit, at all times, the blazing light of
the noon-day sun, that everyone, at any time,
might satisfy himself that all was proceeding
-rightly.
When they aro sold at cost price it is the
interest of one and all to co-operate to lesson
cost. Provide therefore, oh engineers ! all

labour-saving machines to your brother indus-
trials and, remembering all just price is in the
nature and indemnification of damages, where
they cannot purchase, rent your stored-up
labour at a price to reimburse you the wear
and tear, in the same way that the rent of
houses is simply the wear and tear, which
is so much of the stored-up labour expended.
A palatial residence erected, it must not be
managed by a number of persons, not even by
two, confusion would likely at once commence.
Individuality is the lass of order; there must
be one manager only, who, having an account
of each one's contribution, would be the store-
keeper of the stored-up labour in the building.
Ile would appoint, doubtless- consulting the
wishes of his co-operators, the superintendents
of the kitehen and other departments, and
with these each one would make his own
private arrangements; and the manager would
see that no one encroached, and where one
persisted in doing so, he would request him to
leave, handing him the equivalent of his
stored-up labour. _ _ _ _

Competition in the existing social order is
in regard to the means of existence, and is
therefore mostly merciless and destructive,
there being no security of condition for any
class; but under the. reign of equity, compe-
tition would be for superiority of perfor-
mance. In the scramble between wrecked and
struggling sea-farers for places in the lifeJ
boat, we have an illustration of competition
for security of condition. In the generous
emulation between the school-boys, safely '
seated in the pleasure-boat, who think them-
selves most competent to pull at the oar, we
have an illustration of genial and beneficial
competition, competition for superiority viper-
formance ; under such circumstances, whoever
carries off the palm, the interests of the whole
are equally promoted. Understanding this,
the Education Question becomes a very simple
one to settle among yourselves, every work-
shop will become an industrial school and you,
master workmen will be the professors, and
all wanting to learn how to help themselves
will apply to you, like the school-boys applied
to the smart ones, and as your charge will
simply be time and trouble, everyone will be
able to vary his occupation as he feels dis-
posed, and to run in the groove nature intended
him for.

It is robbery of publio property for any one
to appropriate to hinisrlf any natural wealth,
as lands, mines, &0., beyond what ho himself
can work for his own use; and as it is of
little or no value to any one except when
labour is expended upon it, which labour is
entitled to the whole of its results, to prevent
a bloody fight on account of the present mis-
appropriation of natural wealth of the country,
in future every person presenting himself as
a candidate for Parliament should be pledged
to vote the restoration of it to the publio. In
the meantime you will withdraw from
counties or private estates where equity is
considered foolishness.

In every arrangement, of whatever sort,
every one's sovereignty must, at all time, be

respected, like at a recent expected severe

contest at cricket, where one of the chief
players, just before commencing play, with-
drew on account of a relative's - death. Now
suppose a majority of the players considered
such a course wrong, on the ground of what
an individual owed to society (society mean-
ing, in these agitators' view, as it does with
all agitators, themselves, and the mobs they
can get to think with them), and enacted that
on such occasions, under pia of imprison-
ment, a player was on no account to
absent himself: and supposing a player,
so compelled to attend, proceeded very
leisurely after the balls, and the majority
. enacted all players were to proceed after the
balls at a certain pace, would they not,
eventually, enact themselves into endless con-
fusion. An unexpected event has arisen
which has changed the players' relation to the
others, and he alone can decide to what extent
that event affects him. His friends must
only do the next best thing. Respecting the
sovereignty of everyone does not prevent rules
like those of a game being laid down to regu-
late proceedings for any purpose or under-
taking, but the idea must be got rid of that a
man is not capable of governing himself and

hence needs some Other man or mien to govern
him. He is entitled of right to his own self-
government, whether good or bad in the
judgment of others, whenever be exercises it
at his own cost, that is, without encroaching
upon others. In truth, men have rought for
ages the right government, and lo! here it is,
that men cease totally to attempt to govern
each other at all, that they learn to know the
consequences of their own act's, and that they
arrange their relations With each other upon
such a basis that the disagreeable consequences
shall be assumed by the agent himself.. Ileing
simply this, and each county, managing its
own affairs, will not the Houses of Lords or
Commons be soon played out.
Once more about value. A cup of water to
different persons may be of different values
according to the different degrees in which it
is wanted. Hence value in itself is an
element of great uncertainty, but under the
present system of buying and selling, there is
superaddod another element of great uncer-
tainty, the quantity of money, which may be
very plentiful or very source, like the product
of the herring , fishery. Uncertainty end
fluctuation is to measure the prioe of a thing.
To say the least of it, can any system ho more
silly ? but, judging from its results, were the
devil to play hell, could. he devise anything
more atrocious?

W. AUNOLD.

THE PAYMENTS OF WAGES BILL
AND THE AMENDED PAYMENT OF
WAGES BILL.
Tun evils of Truck in this country were felt
so much that, forty years Hp, after a thorough
inquiry into the question, it was prohibited by
law in a large number of trades upon whom it
was then Seen to press heavily and injure by
its degrading tendencies. The Truck Act of
1832 was framed with great care—it was
worded with such exactitude that it was con-
sidered when it passed that it had no loop-
hole for evasion. Unfortunately, Truck was
well-known, and is to this day, to be a source
of great gain (though a.very despicable one),
and there was, therefore, every teMptatiou to
evade it. Truck-loving employers soon found
out low and cunning pettifogging lawyers who
both made the crevices and tried to drive the
team through them. It is to he regretted,
yet it is true as it appear to us, that when
the oases came before our great la* lords, they
took the matter in hand, drove them through
in the most flagrant manner, Setting aside the
clear wording of the. Act, at least in many
ways. In these circumstances it was soon
found the Act was not the boon it was expected.
to be, that the villanous and unscrnpulous
culled on the traffic in open defiance of the
letter of the law, the most sapient law lords
having pronounced in se many ways that gave
the 'Practice full liberty. Appeals have from
time to time. for more than twenty-five years
now been. made to Parliament to make the
law more stringent. The miners, in their
thousands and tens of thousands, by their peti-
tions in 18t50-51-52-63-57-58-59-60-63-04-63
66-68-69-70-7 i, and 72, showed how
deeply they felt injured by its workings.
Others clamoured as well till we had the
question investigated by the Select Committee
that sat on the miners' grievances for three
sessions, and latterly by that searching and
exhaustive Royal Commission that was
appointed by the present Government, and
which, let us only add, did its work so
admirably, and from whose report the Pay-
ment of Wages Bill was framed—a Bill by its
clear, and, so far as we see, distinct provisions
calculated to destroy the remains of th it
vile system which has often made `! the who
and children mourn," from the facilities it
gives to drunkenness and every vile habit that
tends to sink our working-class populations.
That a Bill of this character was likely to
incur opposition was to be looked for ; it was
to destroy a source of gain to the employing
class, or such of them as can pollute the moral.
atmosphere truckhly. Its aim Was to strike
at a monopoly created by the Legislature
to the employing interests,as against, the whole
comminuity, to ensure pay menti (Wall thy rive
to the workmen. The opponents of the Bill
did not meet it with open and avowedLostility
in the House of COMIIIOII3. Mr. G. IlAttnr
took to the nursing of it as if the Haut

SECRETARY had not been able to do that himself.
He was seconded in his efforts in that way by,
that distinguished Liberal, Mr. EDMUND'
POTTER, who graces the Borough of Carlisle
as one of its representatives. He showed such
strong solicitude for its welfare, that in an
evil moment Mr. BRUCE gave it over to their
charge, with a few others, to bring up in a
Select Committee. , From a strong anti-Truck
Bill, by the nursing of the POTTER'S, HARDY'S,
FEILDEN'S, ELLIOT'S, HERMON'S, POWELL'S,
and TRELAWNEY'S, we have got in an Amended
Bill, which, if paved, will prove to be an
excellent Truck promoter. A cursory analysis
of the two Bills will best prove this; what
really relates to Truck divides itself into two
parts, the payment of wages and the deduc-
tions. To enable your readers, so far as I can,
to understand the Bill and the amended one,
I will follow these in their order. •
PAYMENT Or WAGES.—By the Bill intro-
duced by the HOME SECRETARY it was laid down
as a principle that all wages should accrue
from day to day, and then all the workmen
and workwomen to whom the Act would ,
apply should be paid weekly; in the event of
the employer not paying weekly, all persons
employed by him or them should be entitled
to draw on account the Sum of 90 per cont.
up till the end of four weeks, when the '
residue should be paid in full. The Amended
Bill stipulates that the wages of the workmen
shall accrue weekly, and only 76 per cent. to
be drawn on account till the work is finished,
which may be one month, or one year, or ten
years. To make the difference still clearer,
No. 1 Bir makes the provision that wages be
paid weekly. No. 2 Bill does the same. No.
1 Bill makes the balance held by the employer
one day. No. 2 Bill makes the wages always
held by the employer one week, or what is
virtually fourteen days' pay. No. 1 Bill gives
90 per cent. of a draw on account; No. 2.gives
75. No. 1 Bill finds that there cannot be a
balance of ten per cent, longer owing than
four weeks; No. 2 Bill allows 25 per cent. of
the whole earnings to rest in the hands of
the employers, it may be for four years, it may
be for ever, if they so choose to offer their
contract, and the poverty and folly of the
Truck victim compel him to accept the
terms or the contract. One thing more, if
the proposition that is now on the notice
paper by that excellent and esteemed M.P.,
Mr. FIELDEN, should be carried, viz.,
that the pays be fortnightly, then, with the
week still lying in tho hands of the employers,
it will make the pays all three weeks. By all
and on all hands, it is admitted that long
terms of payments is the only way by which
Truck can live and thrive. In thousands of
instances workmen by dint of their combina-
tion have been able to reduce the pays to
weekly. Some noble-hearted employers have
also given their workpeople that boon. In
other cases the workmen have obtained for
themselves by strikes, or concessions by the
employers, the payment of wages every fort-
night. Till now the monthly pays or the
quarterly are far in the minority. Yet in the
face of this, we have an audacious attempt
,on
the part of some of the members of the so-
called people's Parliament to lengthen out the
terms of paying wages by an act of the people's
House.

PAYING WAGE's AT, CoNTlGuous, AND Winlan
INToxicAmo DiaNxs AnE SOLD.—There is no
more disgusting feature of the Truck system
than that of paying workmen near to, or in
liquor steres,:or groceries ; all that have any
c4erience of it know that it, as a rule,
debases males and females all alike. By the
Ti auk Act of 1832, stringent provisions have
becn made against this evil. Many of those
that carried it on became so ashamed of the
traffic that they, to all appearance, gave it up
This was merely in appearance, however. The
Truck Commission brought out the ugly fact
that if they had let their sinks of iniquity and
shame, they drew large revenues from them
in an indirect way. At places we could name
it. was found the rents of these places were
weirething really fabulous. Ey Clause 9 of the
original Bill it
,was worded as to prevent
the paying of workmen contiguous to such
places; by the Amended Bill, it is only pro-
hibited it the employer has a direct interest in
the phial or business, thus laying still

open the door for them that will stoop
to do it to draw princely incomes
from the dissipation of their work-
people. Yet, most of these very men will
prate about "the loose habits" and the intem-
perate habits of the working classes. More
singular still, we know, at least in one case, a
great light among the abstainers supporting
such a state of things.
DEDUCTIONS FD.OU WAGES BY THE Ex-
PLOYERS.—By the Act of 1832, certain de-
ductions were allowed to be kept by the
employers on the condition that the contracts
were signed, and in the handwriting of the
workman. This condition the landlords
quickly set aside, by its being simply the
custom of the district, or colliery, or workshop,
that was necessary. These very deductions
have been a fertile source of Truck, and of
rascality in many forms. The abuses of these
deductions have caused more misery in
many places than anything we know. By
the Bill, deductions were reduced to three—
education, fines, and board and lodging
where the workmen receive such. Against
the first we have little complaint,
only this, that the parent should be allowed
to choose the teachers. By the Amended Bill
the allowed deductions are as folldws :-Ist,
education; 2nd, lines; 3rd, board and lodg-
ing; 4th, advanced money; sth, house rent;
tith, fuel; 7th, medicine; Bth, medical attend-
ance; oth, subscriptions to hospital; 10th,
subscriptions to dispensaries ; 11th, powder;
12th, candles; 13th, picks, dressing or shar-
pening; 14th, lamps; 15th, now tools of
any kind; 16th, cooked food of any kind;
17th, where it is customary for employers to
charge for the tubs, the men are to have the
coal; 18th, wood in the mines where the
miner has to provide his own timber; 20th,
in all the trades to which the Bill applies,
any material given to the workmen by
the employer for payment to carry on
his operation. Now, all the deductions
are looked upon as pernicious. Besides, we
have yet to learn what right any
employer of a workman has a claim to
have his debts paid before any other person—
, the wages that a workman earns ought to be

the common property of all his creditors—as it
is earned to meet his general outlay. No one
should have a preferred claim, least of all the
employer, who, from his very relation to the
workman, stands in a better position than any
other creditor. Holding this view, as we do
firmly, let us see the effect of the 4th deduc-
tion, advanced money. To allow - such a
deduction as this would be to snake virtually
no change on the existing state of things. At
all the Truck
.works, money is advanced now
on the wages—the implied conditions are that
all such money be spent in the store, or
Truck shops. True, both Bills say that it must
not be implied that advanced money on wages
must be spent in the stores. But then, mark,
there is no such condition with advanced
' money not on wages. All that is required is
simply to change the machinery so that
insteadof the Truck victim having wages duo,
let him always have one day's wages or the
ainount of one day's wages in advance, and
then will Truck be in full bloom in its very
worst fem. That might not be at the present,
when there are two masters for one workman;
let man become a drug in the labour market,
and the machinery can easily and will be
changed should such a monstrous proposition
become law. In the hour of commercial dul-
ness the most upright and provident will be
compelled to take to the loan from the employer
to ensure work, and Truck would be as
unchecked as ever. We may be told that
flagrant acts like these we have named would
bring punishments.. We have only to call to
mind the judgments in the case of Mr. INNEs
against the Shotts Iron Company, and many
others; with the existing Truck Act, they
justify our worst fears when the law lords may
have to decide the case.
THE DENTAL 01? THE RIG in .10 SUE
FOIL GOODS.—The Truck Act of 1832 denied
an employer all right to s.astain a suit for
goads that might have been supplied in viola-
tion of the Act. Thk we looked upon as a
penalty that deterred many from trucking that
otherwise might have Hdone. The amended
Bill gives a right to ate to the employer for

some things that he or they may supply that
have been manufactured or adapted for sale on
the premises. Query. We should like much
to know what "adapting for sale on the pre-
mises" means? The firkin of butter is not
adapted for sale to the workman. The
bale of cloth is not adapted to the
use of the workman. The butter con-
verted into a pound makes it adapted
to the use of the workmen—so with the
pound of sugar, so with the yard or two
yards of cloth. With this view, and we believe
it the right one to take, Truck .would be
extended greatly in its operations instead of
checked one point more under this head. Since
the passing of the Truck Act, all payments in
stores, or where goods are sold, were prohibited,
and justly; this Amended Bill proposes that
where goods are manufactured or adapted for
workpeople, they may be paid on the same pre-
mises. To conclude this point, we unhesi-
tatingly say the general tendency of the Bill
will be, if passed into law, to promote the
villanous system of Truck under which so
many thousands of our working classes have
groaned and perished.
One point more; by the Bill it was prohibited
on the part of a workman to assign on mortgage
his wages before they were due. This we
think right, and we see it is continued in the
Amended Bill; but let us simply look how the
Committee had acted previously, they had
allowed to the employer his debt to be paid by
deductions from wages. Was this not a
mortgage—an assignment? How modest!
this in the FIELDEN'S, the POTTEIVS, the
HmtmoN's, the TIIELAWNEY'S, and others. It
was modest, very! to secure all for the
employer; lot the zest scramble for theirs.

The- views we have now stated we believe
to be the true results that would flow from
the Bill as amended if it should become law.
It may be asked what is •to be done to
stay such a thing; it is not for us to say only
in our individual opinion. It will be dealt
with by the Parliamentary Committee we trust;
we would only say this, let every body of
workmen—organised or otherwise,—moot and
send remonstrances by the thousand to the
HomE SECRETARY, calling upon him by amend-
ments to restore the Bill to its original
position before it goes into the committee
of the whole House. Less than this ought not
to satisfy the working classes of this country.

In another letter we will deal with the pro-
ceedings of the committee, giving to each their
proper place for their votes and their agree-
ments in clauses; by this the people will see
their frionds.—Yours,
ALEXANDER MCDONALD,
President, Miners' National Association.

articles.title: BALLOT BILL
articles.text:
THE BALLOT BILL

THE Ballot Bill has now gone through the
Committee of the House of Commons, and it
waits the third reading on the 30th of May.
This is now, therefore, the only opportunity
we shall have to discuss its merits before it be
finally passed or thrown out. Let us, how-
ever, before commenting upon it, enter into a
short analysis of the measure. Tho leading
feature of the Ballot Bill is this—The elector
enters into the polling station, gets from the
presiding officer a Ballot paper, on which is
inscribed the names of all the candidates. He
then enters into a secret compartment, and
there puts 'a mark to the name of the candidate
on the Ballot paper for whom he votes, folds
up the Ballot paper so as to conceal the name
which is marked, returns to the public com-
partment, and then drops his Ballot Paper
into the box.

To iweserve the secrecy of the vote in the
process whieh we have detailed, two things
are absolutely necessary. Ist. No one must
see the elector mark his Ballot paper; and,
secondly, the paper so marked must not be
shown to any one before it be deposited in the
box. If the elector, upon his return from the
secret compartment, opens his Ballot paper,
and shows it to the agents of the different
candidates who are present during the
polling, then_ there is no secrecy and the
Ballot Bill becomes a mere sham and farce.
This was evident to the Government, and Mr.-
LEATThot, with the concurrence of Mr. GLAD-
“TONE and Mr. FoRsIER, propoi;ed as an addi-
tion to the polling clause a severe penalty

upon any elector, who, after marking his
Ballot paper in the secret compartment, wil-
fully opened it out upon his re-entranee into
the public compartment. This amendment,
however, was thrown out by a considerable
majority. So, as the Bill at present stands,
every electors is at full liberty, after marking
his Ballot paper in the secret compartment
of the polling station to open it out in the
public compartment, and to proclaim to every-
one there for whom he has voted. In this way
a dishonest elector after having sold his vote
for a certain price can prove to the agent who
has bribed him, that he has kept his word and
claim the reward promised him. Again by
the Ballot Bill as it now stands, a tyrannical
landlord or employer of labour can insist upon
his tenant or workman displaying
his Ballot
paper after being marked so as to disclose
whether or not he has voted for the candidate
whom the landlord or master favours.

•
By this process of voting, laid down in the
Government Ballot Bill—viz., by marking in
a secret compartment the name of the selected
candidate, it is evident that neither a blind
Toter nor one who cannot read could record his
vote without assistance. We shall now de-
scribe the manner in which the Bill provides
for this. When a blind man enters the
polling booth, the presiding officer marks the
ballot paper in presence of the agents of the
dill'erent candidates, according to the direc-
tions
.from the blind elector. In this case there
is perfect publicity, as much so as exists in
the rade in practice at present at the elec-
tions. It is the same thing with the illiterate
voter. According to the Bill as amended in
Committee, the illiterate elector, after making
; a declaration before a magistrate that he can-
not read or write, records his vote by placing
in the box the ballot paper marked by the pre-
siding officer in presence of the agents of the
candidates. It is thus seen that, according to
the Bill which Government proposes to have
read a third time on the 30th of May, the
electors who can read are allowed to open
their ballot papers before putting them into
the box; in which case the secrecy is merely
permissive, while in the case of the illiterate
the electors are not even allowed a choice, but
are compelled publicly to announce for whom
they vote. We ask once more if this can be
called vote by ballot ? which means the pre-
servation of tho most perfect secrecy as to the
candidate in whose favour the vote is given.
It will, we consider, be a great calamity if this
Bill passes, for it will stand in the way of any
good measure being adopted for many years to
come. The aristocracy, Liberal and Conser-
vative, Who are all opposed to the secret vote,
will do their utmost to prevent any amend-
ment or alteration from being attempted or
introduced. Were we a member of the House
of Commons we should not have the slightest
hesitation in voting against the third reading
of this sham Bill, and we consider that all the
sincere friends of the Ballot in the House of
Commons should do so. Were the Bill thrown
out, Ministers would be compelled to introduce
either this session or the next a real Ballot bill,
and to pledge themselves to dissolve Parliament
should the Government Bill not be carried in
all its integrity. Had they made such a
declaration at the commencement of the
session, the Hanconars and BOUVERIES would
not have dared to join with the Conservatives
in mutilating the Bill, and rendering it, as
they have done, utterly worthless.
We hope that the next time a Liberal Go-
vernment introduces into the House of Com-
mons a Ballot Bill, that Bill will be framed on
a different model from that which it is pro-
posed to read a third time on the
,30th of
May. All that complicated machinery adopted
from Australia, of entering into secret com-
partments to mark the Ballot paper is
unnecessary and absurd, and cannot be carried
out without imposing penalties upon the
elector who opens his Ballot paper when ho
re-enters the public department. It was this
necessity of penalties in order to preserve the
secrecy of the votes, which has given the pro-
fessing Liberals, who are the secret enemies o•
f
the Ballot, an excuse for mutilating the
• Government measure. We are astonished
• that Mr. FOICSTER and Mr. GLABSIONE did not
• frame the Ballot Bill upon that model with
which 41. Members of Paliament are perfootlY

familiar, and. which is constantly passing
under their eyes—upon the model of vote by
Ballot in every club in London.
Let us see the manner ef electing members
for the Reform Club. 'We shall say it would
answer for the election of members of the
House of Commons. At every polling station
there would be a number of ballot boxes equal
to the number of the candidates. Those
ballot boxes, according to their construction
in every club in London, would be divided
into two compartments, right and left, but not
seen from without, with an orifice into which
the voter could put his hand and by the feel
could distinguish the right hand compartment
from the left. On the ballot boxes would be
written the names of the different candidates
—each name on a separate box. And there
would in addition be written on the right
side of the box "Yes," and on the left side
"No," to mark that a ball put in the
right side compartment would be a vote
for that candidate whose name was on the box
and a ball on the left would bo against him.
When the polling took place, the elector on
entering the station, and after verifying his
right to vote, would receive a ball from the
presiding officer to put into each box
respectively; no instruction would require
to be given him, as the writing on the
ballot box would explain everything. When
the elector could not read, the presiding
officer would, in presence of the agents of the
candidates, explain to him the manner in which
he should vote, and would read over to him
the name of the different candidates, leaving
him to decide in which box he would place the
ball which gave the vote. The secrecy of
the vote would. thus be perfectly preserved,
while at the same time it would be impossible
for a corrupt voter to prove to a bribing agent
in what manner he had voted; and even the
blind elector would vote according to this form,
without being obliged to make known to any
one how he had voted. All that would be
required in his case would be for the presiding
officer to give him a ball for each box, and to
place his hand in the orifice leaving him
to drop the ball into the right or left compart-
ment according as he wished to vote for or
against the candidate. I mentioned the other
day this mode of voting by ballot, which I
considered a perfect one, to a friend of mine,
the Secretary of the Greek Embassy at Lon-
don. To my surprise, he informed me that
that was precisely the manner which had
been always followei in Greece, And which he
assured me had been found to answer per-
fectly. %TIMES AYTOUN.

THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACTS.
IT is not for the purpose of arguing with
Dr. HUMPHREY SANDWITH, holding the
peculiar views of justice and morality that he
describes himself as holding, that I wish, with
your permission, to say something on this
subject, but in order to ask him to complete
some of the statements which ho has com-
menced in his very instructive letters. He
has told us the haV of several things—will he
be good enough to tell us the other half, that
we may the hotter judge of the merits of his
ease ?

Dr. &N Ml= makes many assertions of
fact and of principle, but he always leaves
out, in a very tantalising way, something that
is necessary to enable one to arrive at an
opinion on the whole case, or to understand
what he really does mean. Challenged to
explain what he meant by the words "no
natural function can be suppressed, and the
system of regulating this function by marriage
under immense difficulties which it obtains in
our form of civilisation is a very imperfect
one," and asked whether he meant that
"marriage was out of date, and that the
relations of the sexes should henceforth rest
on a system of bettor regulated prostitution,"
he indignantly scorns the imputation, and
says that he would meet the difficulty "by
increased facilities of marriage and by other
means," but he does not say what the other
means are that are not marriage, nor better
regulated prostitution, nor—for that is not to
be thought of—repression of natural impulses.
The impulse, we are told, is irrepressible,
and so must be gratified; but he stops short
and omits to flay how, at what cost. Who,

that hears the jaunty way in which he says
that it must be, could imagine that the admir-
able propensity demands the sacrifice of
another human life and, a human soul to
gratify it?

Again, he tells us that "the villain who
pollutes his neighbour's bed, or who de-
liberately and. diabolically seduces innocent
maidens" escapes the disease; b tit once more
his story is unfinished in the most tantalising
Way—he does not tell us whether the neigh-
hour's wife and the maiden escape, or why
they are not to be protected. Besides, the
expression "the :villain who diabolically
seduces innocent maidens" puzzles me. Why
villain? It is surely hard to call him names.
He has natural impulses—which surely are
human, not devilish, Dr. SANDIVITII ?—that
must not be repressed; he is not to gratify
them at the expense of his neighbour's wife;
the present supply of "hardened prostitutes "
' will die off some day if nobody seduces
innocent maidens. It seems to me that there
is a bad time coming for owners of irresistible
impulses in the future.
We know why the neighbour's wife is to be
respected—not because she is a woman, but
because the neighbour is a man and must not
be wronged. We might wonder why the
maidens should not be seduced, but Dr. Sun-
WITH has helped. us here. In another passage
he says "the wives and. children of guilty
men are themselves the children or near
relatives of innocent men," and, therefore are

to be protected at the cost of innocent men
(though who can be innocent men Dr.
SANDWITII makes it rather difficult to under-
stand). So perhaps the maidens in question are
to be respected because they "belong "to some
man. But then comes the question, are the
hardened ivostitutes the near relatives of any-
one but themselves? If it should prove that
they are, I find myself in this difficulty
The impulse cannot be repressed.
But it must not be indulged
1. At the expense of neighbour's wives,
2. At that of innocent maidens, i.e.,
neighbour's daughters.

There remains a class on whom it may be
ndulged, namely hardened prostitutes; but
lien is a possibility that they are neighbour's

daughters too, so that / cannot see by what
laufid prooess hardened prostitutes come into

existence. Can Dr. SANDWITII tell me, are
they spontaneously generated ? or by what

_
process not involving the intervention, and
the guilty intervention, of men, do maidens

ever cease to be innocent, and thus become the
lawful prey of men?
Without these explanations I am at present
forced to conclude that, in common with all
pro-Acts people, Dr. SANDWITIL leaves out
of consideration or denies the fact that
the victims of the Acts are human beings
just as much as the "unfortunate youths "
and " profligate husbands" whom he is so
careful of, and to protect whom in the exercise
of their undoubted rights, the undoubted
rights of other human beings are to be, he
asserts, as a matter of course, sacrificed. If
profligate men are to be protected from disease,
so too, it seems to me, must profligate women
be. The special police are always telling us
what numbers of them marry. Are not their
innocent husbands and children worth a
thought? Are men to be at liberty to infect
them with impunity ?

Again, if the wives and children of profligate
men are to be protected, a readier way though
doubtless less pleasant to our male lawgivers
coull be found, since, as Dr. SANDWITII says,
nearly all men are more or less profligate." Few,''
we are told, " can afford to throw stones."
Since a single " error " of a " poor lad " may
injure him for life and make him liable to in-
jure others, it follows that it is absolutely
necessary for the safety of innocent wives and
children that no man should be allowed to
marry without satisfying a State-appointed
functionary that ho is and always has been
free from this disease. Moreover, as the
right of British husbands to commit adultery
ad libitum is being so boldly proclaimed, it
would follow that every man living with his
wife should undergo periodical inspection for
her safety. When •we see men taking these
natural precautions for that end, we will believe

that the acts are invented in the interest of the

innocent, and not before.
We maintain that all women are human
beings, even prostitutes ; that the latter are
not one bit worse than the men who seek them ;
if their life is evil, what are the men who hire
and bribe them to adopt it? That, as between
these guilty men and women it is monstrous
to sacrifice the human and civil rights of the
one to the physical comfort of the other; that
the women never injure the innocent; and that
the men could be far more effectually, as well
as more justly hindered from doing so, in the
way above described.
In conclusion, let me say, that I foresee
danger from a too ready acceptance of Dr.
SANDWITIL'S doctrine that "no natural func-
tion can be suppressed "—especially if it were
to be accepted by women, as why should it
not, if it be true? We are recommended, on
the plea that, it is their nature, to "let dogs
(and other animals) delight to bark and bite,"
and this is all very well, as long as they bark
at and bite each other, but when their fierce
propensities threaten the welfare or safety of
human beings, human beings are apt to sup-
press them. So if we really are to accept Dr.
SANDWITIL'S teaching, which amounts to this,
that men are noxious beasts whose existence is
incompatible with women's safety, women,
being human beings, may take to suppressing
the noxious beasts. Unless the beasts repress
themselves there will be blood shed over this
matter yet.

LUCY WILSON.

articles.title: TELE CURRENCY QUESTION.
articles.text:
TELE CURRENCY QUESTION.

As the organ of the working class you,
and you alone of all the London press, have
always advocated the necessity of having a
fair inquiry into the present system which
currency reformers denounce as being a
swindle upon the working class, often
limiting and sometimes preventing their
obtaining that employment by which alone
they can obtain wages to procure food for
themselves and families; and to prove the
sincerity of their convictions, all they ask is
for a fair and public inquiry by Select Com-
mittees of both Houses of Parliament, and.
this Mr. GLADSTONE refuses to grant.
In this refusal he is perfectly aware he is
backed by the very rich and, their parasites
in the press, who affect to treat the question
as settled, as witness the deliberate falsehood
of Mr. MURRAY, of Mr. MoRLEY (which I
have lately expressed in the columns of the
BEE-HivE), of the Oxford Professor of Political
Economy at Liverpool, and of Mr. WALTER
Of the Times.

Writing in favour of the present system,
Mr. WALTER asserted—" That not an idea can
be introduced, nor a difficulty suggested on this
question, which has not already been sifted and
answered with wearying iteration." As soon
as this assertion was brought to my attention
(for a gentleman need not read the Times in
the country), I thought it right to call the
attention of Mr.
.WALTER, the member for.
Berkshire, and the principal proprietor of the
Times, in a letter, from which the following
is an extract:—" As it is very probable that
the paragraph which I have quoted from your
paper has escaped your notice, it would be
most unfair for me to assume that you have
wilfully permitted a newspaper, of which you
are the principal proprietor, to state, without
rebuke, a wilful and deliberate falsehood upon
a, subject of the highest importance to the
people, and deeply affecting the employment,
and therefore the food, of themselves and

To this letter Mr. WALTER never replied
and therefore I again wrote to him exposing
the cowardly meanness of his conduct. My
letter also enclosed 19 separate propositions
of the Currency reformers, which had never
been answered or even noticed either in the
columns of the Times or elsewhere; the cor-
respondence and propositions are inserted
verbatim (page 43) in the pamphlet entitled,
"Necessity of Altering OW Monotaty Laws,
proved from the highest monetary autho-
rities : " the letters were written in 1871, and
published on May 20th, 1871.

Thus, iii May, 1871, 'but " mayna est veritas
et prevalebit," yet, no one could have expected
that oven the Times 't would have turned about

and jump Jim Crow " in so short a time upon
the most important quest ion affecting the best
interests of the working class; but this
identical Mr. WAITER, still principal pro-
prietor of the Times, published the following
critique upon the Querist:—" The Querist•
contains more home truths than were ever before
or since compiled in so brief a compass." ,
Home truths forsooth ! Why, they contain

the identical truths which myself and other
currency reformers have been advocating for
years past, and which Mr. WALTEu, in the
passage which I have quoted, so falsely declared
"had been 4fted and answered with wearyiny
iteration." Now, the Times distinctly says :-
Ist. That the prejudices about gold and
silver are very strong, but they arc still pre-
judices.

2nd. That our prejudices about gold are very
apt to infect or misguide our judgments and
reasonings against the public weal.

3rd. That the abuse of banks and paper-
money is no just objection to the use thereof,
for such abuse might be easily prevented.
4th. That a bank of national credit, sup-
ported by public fund, and secured by Parlia-
ment, is no chimera or impossible thing.
sth. That the currency of credit so well
secured would be of great advantage to our
trade and manufactures.

Gth. That a view of the ruinous effects of
absurd schemes and credit mis-managed,—so
as to produce gaming and madness, instead of
industry, can be no just objection agaiiast a
national bank calculated purely to promote
industry.
7th. That we are not sufficiently sensible of

the peculiar security thbre is in having a ,bank
that consists of lani ana papers—one of whieli
cannot be exported, and the other is in no
danger of being experted.
The writer of the money artiole in the
Times will open his eyes when he reads this
article.

May 20, 1872.

RIGBY W.LON.

DR. SANDWITH AND THE SHIELD.
Dn. SANiIWITII has fallen itito a carious
mistake in his letter published in your paper
of the 'llth inst., a mistake which he might
have avoided if ho had over read " the wild
articles in the Shield." That paper is the
organ of the National Association for the
repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts, with
whose lady members he is so very indignant.
He attributes to those ladies "a burning rage
for the punishment of those sins for which
they feel no inclination," and quotes the
following words in proof of his assertion:
" Syphilis is the proper punishment of incon-
tinent wen ; if in punishing such men a number
of innocent beings are also immolated, well, so
much the worse for the innocent beings." He
further says: We are bid not to meddle with
the foul disease that infects soeiety from thole
brothels, lest we interfere with the liberty and
modesty of these strumpets."
I appeal to Dr. SANDWITIt'S courtesy to do
me, a member of the association for the repeal
of the Contagious Diseases Acts, the favour of
informing me from which of our publications
he quoted ,the very immoral words he has
placed in inverted commas ; or to name any of
our publications in which he can point out any
words to the same effect ; or any words which
declare that we ought not "to meddle with
the foul disease that infects society." He will
not find any such words or ideas in the ".wild
articles of the Shield," nor in any publication.
authorized by our association. From the
Shield, however, he will learn that our asso-
ciation constantly pleads for the admission of
ll sufferers from venereal disease into all our
hospitals, and that so for front desiring the
punishment of the victims of this disease, our
complaint against the Government Lock
Hospital is, that the method by whieh
women are hounded into them and treated
when there, is a cruel punishment, inflicted on
the weaker sex; While we would desire that
both sexes should be cured as painlessly and
mercifullypossible. It is illogical in Dr.
sN vl:
i u at: blame the imaginary ladies of
lhis own creation " who spurned, frail women
with contumely," while ho himself applies to
such women the contumelious epithets of
strnmpets," and " foul-mouthed, brazen-
faced harlots."

It is not for one of the inferior se'l to judge
whether "the demands of human nature "are
so " imperious " in the superior sea, .as Dr.
SANDWITII declares. I will, for the moment,
accept his assertion as fact. But, in that ease,
why callthe women who supply the imperious
demands of the superior (!) human animal
by such very harsh names? Hunger is an
imperious demand of human nature; but Dr.
SANDWITII does not heap abuse upon bakers.
It would be curious to hear Dr. SANDWITIO3
idea of the nature of the Creator of a race of
beings, the imperious natural demands of one
half of which are so vile and hideous, that the
mere:fact of supplying them necessarily con-
veils the other half (unless
.saved by the
vicarious sacrifice of a Pariah portion of it)
Into creatures so degraded, that Dr. SAND.
WIIII cannot speak of them with compoSure,
and whose diseases (inflicted upon them by
the imperious demands of the stronger animal)
may not be gently ettred out, as human suffer-
ing should be, but must be "stamped out,"
even at the cost of stamping out their woman-
hood also.

I should like to ask Dr. SANDWITH whether
he really believes such to be the mutually
noxious nature bestowed by the Deity upon
the human creatures he has destined to live
together? and whether, holding that belief,
he finds it possible to address that Deity as
our FATHER who art in heaven? I feel very
sure, however, that Dr. SIN DWITH believes
nothing of the kind. There was one man at
least, in the old common days, able, to assert
the dignity of self-sacrifice, and to carry it to
a point of heroic devotion seldom surpassed;
and J hardly think Dr. SAN DWITH can have
forgotten that man, since I have not. But he
is simply very angry with us, and (as the
superior animal is too apt to do) he yields to
the "imperious demands" of his natural in-
dignation at seeing his inferiors rebel. And
reading his letter by this light I can see that
we are not so far apart as he supposes. He
believes "that it is true morality to do our
utmost in exterminating a fell disease which is
eating into the vitals of society," and so do
we.

He would not leave the "poor creatures,'
to whom he gives'sueh hard names, "wallow
ing in vice and disease ;" nor would we.
He would "briny them within the pale of

humanity by a little wholesome coercion."
We would keep them within the pale of
humanity by a little, still more wholesome,
kindness.

The difference between us is, therefore, of
methods, not of aim; and perhaps, if Dr.
SANDWITIT, instead of creating "phenomenal"
ladies out of his own brain, who "gathered
up the skirts of their robes," and "when a
poor sister fell, did their utmost to thrust her
down yet deeper into the mire," would hear
what we women really have to say, he would
discover that our most heartfelt wish is to
help our sisters out of the mire both of disease
and oontempt, and might even find it possi-
ble, with the help of a little forbearance on
both sides, to come to some agreement with us
as to methods, since, it seems, we are already
agreed as to aim.

E. A. VENTURI.

Association for the Repeal of the Contagious
Diseases Acts, 50, Great Ilarlborough-st.

articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

• The mistress at the Roman Catholic Schools,
High-street, Deptford, was on Tuesday charged
at the Greenwich Police-court with having
cruelly beaten a child between six and seven
years of use. The evidence, however, was of
such a character as to satisfy the magistrate
that any injury from which the child might
have suffered was not caused by the chastise-
ment administered by the defendant, and the
summons was therefore dismissed,

At the Thames Police-court on Tuesday, a
manufacturing chemist, carrying on business
in St. Mary Axe, Was fined £2O for having
shipped a case of dangerous liquid without
specifyi_ng the nature of contents.

Last week the mortality in. London and
twenty other large towns in the -United King-
dom was at the rate of 23 deaths annually to
every 1,000 persons estimated to be living. In
the metropolis 2,150 births and 1,268 deaths
were registered, the former having been 95,
and the latter 162 below the average. Fifty-
four persons died from small-pox, 47 from
measles, 16 from scarlet fever, 5. from
diptheria, 73 from whooping cough, 25 from
different form of fever (of which 2 were certi-
fied as typhus, 11 as enteric or typhoid, and
12 as simple continued fever), and 14 from
diarrlicea. The mean temperature was only
47.5, and 4.5 below the average for the corre-
sponding week in fifty years; the mean was
54.1 on Thursday and slightly in excess, while
on Saturday it was only 41.4, and 11,5 below
the average. The deaths referred to diseases
of the respiratory organs, including phrhists,
were 398 and 11 below the corrected average
weekly number.

It is remarked by the Registrar-General in
ins return that the fatal cases of small-pox,
which in the two previous weeks had been 62
and 39, rose again last week to 51, of which
23 occurred in the special small-pox. hospitals,
against 17 and 15 in the two preceding weeks.
Out of those institutions, three deaths each
from this disease were returned in West
Hackney, Poplar, and Waterloo-road second
sub-districts.

On Tuesday evening the annual meeting
of the Peace society was held in Finsbury
Chapel, Mr. Samuel Bowly in the chair. The
report, while acknowledging the disappoint-
ment oocasioned by
.the delay in carrying out
the Treaty Of Washington, expressed satisfac-
tion at the patience and mutual goodwill
manifested by the two great English-speaking
nations on both sides of the Atlantic. In
the course of the, evening sanguine opinions
were expressed respecting the success of the
Society's object.

On Tuesday the annual Moveable Com-
mittee of the Manchester Unity of Odd
Fellows, reassembled at Lancaster. Mr.
Lyulph Stanley, an assistant cotnraissioner of
the Friendly Societies' Commission, attended
the meeting.

Judge Keogh will give his decision in the
Galway election inquiry on Friday.

An underground rocket, commonly known
as the " fish torpedo," has been privately
tried on the canal at Woolwich Arsenal, and
the result is said to have been satisfactory.

At a meeting of the Left Centre party, of the
French Assembly, held on Saturday last, it
was resolved that M. Rouber should be listened
to in profound silence. The members of the
Left who were present moved that the question
should be met by an order of the day, blaming
the Empire. A deputation from the Right
Centre, which attended the meeting by invita-
tion, wished the Government of the ,National
Defence to come in for a Lir share of censure
as well. Ultimately it was arranged that M.
Rouher's question should be shelved by the
order of the day.

At the Bow-street Police-court, on Monday,
Mr. Herbert Crellin, comedian at the Lyceum
Theatre, was charged with creating a dis-
turbance, and annoying Mr, H. L. Bateman,
the lessee. The defendant had entered into an
engagement to perform at the Lyceum only,
and when he was asked to go with the com-
pany to Manchester lie declined. A document
was then, handed him to sign, terminating his
engagement. It was then that he spoke
strongly to Mr. Bateman, who gave him into
custody for annoyinghim. The complainant had
left for Manchester, and the matter was ad•
journetl in order that it might be fully
investigated.

A gentleman was summoned at the Wands-
worth Police-court, on Monday, by one of his
domestic servants for having. assaulted her.
The defendant had entered the servants' bed-
room to make inquiries respecting a candle
which had disappeared from his own apart-
ment, and on the cOmplamant remonstrating,
he struck her. The magistrate characterised
the assault as a trumpery one, and ordered the
dEfon,lent to pay only the cost of the summons

A lady at Notting-hill, returning from a
drive, found the housemaid confused, the
cookinebriated, the sideboard open, and the
spirit bottles empty. The cock, admitting she
had taken some of their contents, was com-
mitted at Hammersmith for fourteen days with
hard labour.

The suspension is reported at Devonport of
the Western Permanent Equitable Building
Society, through some defalcations of the
chairman. An attenipt will be made to tide
over the difficulty and prevent the forced
realisation of the society's property.

A man, who described himself as a cooper's
labourer, was on Tuesday sentenced to six
months' imprisonment, with hard labour, by
the Southwark police magistrate for having
committed a brutatassault Upon his wife. At
the same court three months of, the like pun-
ishment were awarded to a man who had
beaten a female companion with whoin., he
had been on terms of intimacy.

A boy twelve years of age, who bore a very
bad. character, was on Monday sent to an
Industrial School for four years by the Wands-
worth police magistrate, for having violently
assaulted. his father with two blacking
brushes, while the latter, an' invalid, was
lying in bed suffering from an attack of rheu-
matic gout.

Dr. Whittemore preached on Wednesday the
annual "Flower Sermon," at the• Church of
St. Katherine Cree, in presence of a large con-
gregation, all the younger members of which
carried bouquets.

Samuel Johnson, a youth of eighteen, son
of a grocer, carrying on business at Wednes-
bury, was drowned on Sunday night at
Leamington. He had joined a party of ex-
oursioxists in a trip up the river Learn, and
started on in a canoe, leaving his friends to
follow in a boat. When the party reached a
spot known as the Big Island, they found the
canoe empty, and Johnson's hat floating down
the river. The police were engaged dragging
the river up to a late hour, but failed to
recover the body.

From April Ist to the 18th inst. the Exchequer
receipts amounted to £9,499,623, an increase
of nearly £1,800,000 upon the revenue in
the corresponding period of last year. The
expenditure has been £10,053,029. On Satur-
day last the balance in the Bank of England
was £6,927,160.

A rough-looking fellow, who gave the name
of Martin Birmingham, was on Monday charged
at the Marylebone Police-court with having
annoyed a church congregation in Carlisle-
street, Lisson-grove. The Rev. Dr. Spencer
gave evidence of the defendant's bad conduct,
and in default of finding sureties to keep the
pew:mile was sent to prison. At Clerkenwell
some youths, who bad been guilty of disorderly
conduct in the I-hill:way -road on Sunday
evening; were fined in small sums.

During the Session of the Methodist Dis-
trict Meeting in Belfast, the Rev. Wm. Crook,
D.D., introduced the Rev. 11, W. Holland, of.
Leeds. The chairman bade Mr. Holland wel-
come,
and said they wore all exceedingly
glad see him. They owed him a. deep
debt of gratitude for the noble stand he had
taken on the . education question. He
thoroughly understood their position; and had
served the cause of truth to an extent to which
he (the chairman) could not venture to. give
expression. Denominational education would
be fatal to the interests of true religion in this
country. He had to thank Mr Holland for
the service he bad rendered the cause of united
secular and separate religious education. Mr.
Holland, after thanking Dr. Scott for his
remarks, said he thoroughly believed deno-
minational education would be a grand blunder
for Ireland.

The Corporation of Dublin lately passed a
resolution in which that body expressed a hope
to see the Princess Louise and the Princess
Beatrice on the Occasion of the approaching
visit of the Puke of Edinburgh to that city.
A reply has been received conveying the regret
of her Majesty that the wish of the Corporation
could not be Complied with. The engagements
of the Princess Louise Would prevent her going
to Ireland at the time named, and the Princess
Beatrice was too young for ceremonials of the
nature foreshadowed.

On Tuesday the Xing of the Belgians, after
visiting Christ's -Hospital, the Corporation
Middle Class Schools, the Gladstone-buildings,
and Columbia-market, received a deputation
from ,the Executive Committee of the Anglo-
Belgian Prize Fund, to whom his Majesty
expressed his interest in that organisation, and
his desire that English Volunteers should again
visit Belgium.

An Eight Hours League in the United
States is announced to have come to a satis-
factory agreement • with the masters in the
building trades. It is being largely joined by
workmen.

A telegram from Geneva announces that the
Prince and Princes of Wales have arrived
there on their way to Paris and intend to
stay for four days.

Monday was the working man's holiday,
and as the weather was bright and. sunny,
with afresh breeze from the south-east, ira,-
metise numbers left London in all directions
for the various places of suburban resort. The
throngs in quest of reoreation stood .thickly
upon the decks of the river steamboats; they
besieged the stations upon the metropolitan
lines of railway; and they filled the omnibuses.
upon every road leading out of the metropolis.
By general consent no, previous holiday has
been more generally observed, not only in the
City, but throughout the entire capital. At
some places, such as, for instance, at the Welsh
Harp, at lendon, the number of sightseers
was unprecedented. There the. Cumberland,'
and Westmoreland Wrestling Society held a
supplementary meeting,
.and although the
competitors were not of the. first rank, the
contests were watched with interest, and the ,
meeting was a great suceess. There were
nearly 45,000 visitors to the Zoological
Gardens, aud more than 21;000 to the
Exhibition.

On Monday, at the Thames Police-court,
there were two cases in which assaults upon
constables were dealt with. In one of these a
woman named Phcebe Ratford, who, on the
morning of the 7th inst. made such a violent '
onslaught upon a police officer, as to incapa-
citate him from duty since, was sent to prison
for three months with hard labour. In the
other, one Patrick Marney, for a brutal attack'
upon a policeman, was awarded six weeks of
the like punishment.

A congress of law students was opened on
Tuesday at Birmingham, when papers were
read and discussions took place on legal edu-
cation, law reform, and cognate topics. The
foundation of a school of law was advocated,
and a resolution passed in favour of the scheme
of legal instruction proposed by Sir Roundell
Palmer, on condition that the Inns of Court
and the Incorporated Law Society should be
affiliated with the school, and that due pro-
vision be made for the praotioal training of
articled clerks,

M a'Hareourt, the new French Minister, at
St. Jamas, has taken leave of President
Thiers, preparatory to starting for London.

Canon Girdlostone has delivered farewell
address to the labourers at Ealberton, in
which he recommended unionism as the only
means of advancing their wages, abolishing
truck, and improving their cottages. He added
a new point to the Arcadian charter in deolar-
ing that every rateable cottage should confer
a vote.

" Died from exhaustion tbrough want of
food and proper nourishment" WWI the verdict
of a coroner'S jury at an inquest held on the
body of James Sewington, farm labourer,
employed at the County Lunatic, Asylum,
Wandsworth. Deceased sometimes earned
iBs, per week, but .in rainy, weather this
amount was considerably reduced, and, as a
consequence, he found his rent in arrear, and
his wife and family almost without food.
Anxious to get out of debt, and to support
those who were dependent upon him, Sewing-
ton deprived himself of the food necessary to
sustain life.

Official aecounta from Spain.make the bold
assertion that Biscay has been paeilled with-
out fighting, and the Carlist Junta which con-
trolled the insurrection dispersed. Aguirre's
defeat has been followed by wholesale sub-
missions. Some of the• fugitives have escaped
into Navarre, and ore vainly endeavouring to
raise the popalation of that province. A rising
was reported at Huesca; but reliable evidence
is still wanting of its reality. Senor Bias has
not condoned the alleged partiality shown to
the Carlists by the French authorities on the
frontier. He stated in the Cortes, in answer
to Senor Casalas's interpellation, that a few
instances had occurred in which protests.were
necessary.

Ministers must be difficult to find at the
Hague, for the King of the Netherlands will
not permit his present advisers to resign. He
has induced them to continue in office until
the War Budget is passed.

M. Greco's murderers are being tried in the
usual Fretieh style at Marseilles, by personal
examination. Sitbon and Sigourr both'
asserted that they had been only indirect ao- -
coraplices, in so far as they kept watch outside
the house. The medical evidence controverted '
,
this defence by tending to prove the presenoe
of more than one participator at the 'murder.

There are indications that IL Thiers is leans
Lug to expect less of his own way from the
Assem i
bly. On the Army Bill he s said t 0
have made a vital conoession by relinquishing
bit opposition to compulsory service. The
discussion of this bill will commence on
day next. next.

A telegram from Rome states that the
Burmese embassy, on its return for Naples
asked for an audience of the Pope. His
Holiness expressed his willingness to receive
the members provided they were not accom-
panied by Captain Ilacehite of the Italian
navy, who has hitherto attended them. The
But mese refused to comply with this
condition, and left Rome for London.

A. Bill has been read in the. Spanish
Parliament fixing the number of men liable
for military service this year at 40,000. It
would appear that there is no truth in the
report of Marshal Serrano having been de-
feated in Biscay by the Carlist insurgents.
The Marshal continnes, it is asserted, to carry
on his operations with complete success.

It has been decided that Marshal Bazaine
is to be tried in the Riding School at
Versailles instead of the Palace, and work-
men are already preparing the place for the
proceedings. 'This latter fact is considered to
throw doubt on the statement that the trial
will not come off for three or four months.

It is stated in a Washington telegram that
the Committee on Foreign Relations has re-
solved to report in favour of the Additional
Article to the Treaty of Washington. Many
addresses recommending the ratification of
the Article have, it is said, been forwarded to
the Committee and to the Senators by bankers
and commercial companies..

A special telegram from Paris states that
although, owing to the threatening weather,
there was not a large attendance at the
Chantilly races on Sunday, the sporting world
mustered in force, and there was good sport
The Freneh Oaks, or Prix de Diane, was won
by the Duke of 'Hamilton's Little Agnes.

On Saturday evening the Duke of
Edinburgh, following the example set by so
many illustrious personages' was admitted
to the Livery of the Worshipful Company of
Fishinongers. The ceremony was succeeded'
by a banquet, at which his Royal Highness,
the Duke of Cambridge, the Lord Chancellor,
the Archbishop of York, and Mr. 13oUverie,
M.P., were amongst the speakers.

Only two cases from Victoria Park were on
Tuesday before the Worship-street magistrate
as the result of Whit-Monday enjoyments.
In one of these two rough-looking men,
named Ferdinando and Bradford, were sen-
tenced -to two months' imprisonment, with
bard labour, for having been guilty of some
represenbensible horse-play. The other was
a charge of theft, which was punished with
four months' hard labour.

There was a further investigation at the
Marlborough-street Police-court on Tuesday
of the charge against a young gentleman
named Remington, of having obtained money
by false pretences from one Bernard Engel.
The 'defendant's mother having been called as
a witness by the counsel for the prosecution,
another remand was applied for and granted.

Mr. John Platt, the. jnnior Liberal member '
for Oldham, died suddenly
.in Paris on &tar-
day from an attack of apoplexy. The deceased,
who was 54 years of age, was twice mayor of
the borough which ho represented, and tilled
the office of High Bheilff of Carnarvonshire in
1863. Be entered Parliament in 1865, when
he defeated Mr.
•blia Morgan Cobbett, who
had. sat for the town during thirteen years.
In 1868, upon Mr. .Disraeli's appealing to the
country on the, Irish Church question' Old-
ham was the scene of one of the fiercest con-
tests which took place even in Lancashire. Mr.
}Ebbed, the present Parliamentary Secretary
to the Local Government Board, plied 6,140
votes; Mr. Platt closely followed with 6,122;
Mr. Cobbett, who now came forward as. a Con-
servative, was only six behind Mr. Platt
while Dr. spinks, his colleague in defeat
mustered 6,084. The sitting members sue-
°awfully defended their seats against a
petition and a scrutiny. The loss of Mr. Platt
will be regretted in the House of Commons,
for he was one of the most earnest and con siS-
tent Liberals in that assembly.

The Marquis of Lorne in presidink at the
annual dinner of the Artists' General Benevo-
lent Institution, earnestly advocated its claims,
pointing out the value of the charity, and at
the same time laying emphasis upon the small
working cost of its management. Subscrip-
tions amounting to more than £2,500 were
announced.
