The Cunard steamier Tripoli, which lately
struck on
,the South Tuscar Rocks, has accord-
ing to a telegram from Wexford, become a
total wreck.

At tho Marlborough-street Police-court on
Saturday, the charge of bigamy against a man
75 years of age, calling himself the lion.
Henry Seymour,- was again proceeded with.
Miss Pugh, the prosecutrix, was examined,
and some letters written to her by the prisoner
Were read. Mr. Knox sent the ease for trial.

Lord Orkney's bankruptcy is t,obe annulled,
official sanction having been given to an
arrangement made by the creditors to accept
a composition of 53, in the pound.

Another companion of street thieves was on
Tuesday brought up at the Southwark Police-
court for having threatened a witness who
had given evidence against the women Lynch
and Murray, who were lately sentenced to
penal servitude for life for shockingly ill-
treating Susan Snellgrove. The prisoner was
ordered to find two sureties to keep the
peace.

A mendicant who called himself Joseph
Smith was on Tuesday sentenced to six weeks'
hard labour by the Lambeth Police magistrate
for having violently assaulted a constable who
had taken him into custody at ihe instance of
an officer belonging to the Charity Organisa-
tion Society.

,
A City trader, who had Obtained possession
of a quantity of tobacco and cigars without
the payment of the Custons duty, has been
ordered by the presiding magistrate at the
Mansion-house to pay the treble value of the
articles and the duty, amounting to nearly
£250, or to be imprisoned until that sum Is
paid.

A supplement to the London Gazette con-
tains additional correspondence between Great
Britain and the United States on the subject
of the claims for indirect losses submitted by
the latter to the Geneva Tribunal. The series
of despatches ranges in• date from the 3rd of
February to Monday last, the 13th instant.
The correspondence is completed by the publi-
cation of the text of the Additional Article to
the Treaty of Washington, which was issued
from the Foreign Office on Tuesday night.

Resolutions in support of President Grant
have ben passed by the Republican Conven-
tions of Michigan and Nebraska. Mr. Horace
Greeley, meanwhile, is said to be gaining
ground among the Democrats.

A correspondent at Smyra sends an account
of the riots which recently took plaee there
between, the Greeks and Jews. The riots
arose out of the prevalent Eastern superstition
that the Jews mix the Mood of Christian
children in the unleavened bread for the Pass-
over rites. As it happened, the body of a
Christian child which had been missing since
the previous day was washed up by the sea. A
report at once spread that its jugular vein had
been divided, and the excitement among the
Greeks soon manifested itself. The Jews
wherever met were ill-treated, and two of
them wore murdered. The victims were old
women, and are said to have defended them-
selves with much bravery. It was not until
the garrison of the town-300 strong—and
other forces had been called out that the riots
were put down,

A report on the state of the Turkish Empire
has been laid before the Sultan by the °rand
Vizier. It gives an exceedingly favourable
picture of the progress of the country, and
especially refers to the means of defence. The
military forces are said to comprise a reserve
of 800,000 men, and the iron-clad navy is so
powerful that Turkey may now be regarded,
the report says, as a first-class-maritime power.
Education is aivanoing, and railway communi-
cation is being extended. The Sultan, in reply,
expressed his dissatisfaction with the state of
the finances. ,

The protest forwarded to the Foreign-oilloe
by the local authorities of Dover against the
landing of expatriated French Communists at
that port has elicited ,a reply from Mr. Ham-
mond, who states that our Ambassador at
"has, received. instructions upon the
subject."

In a report from the chief medical officer of
the Hampstead Hospital,: Which was read at
the meeting of the Metropolitan Asylums
Board on Saturday, it was stated that of
6,221 patients received into the institution
since the • commencement of the small-pox
epidemic 1,248 were unvaccinated. Of these
638, or M. 12 per cent., died, whilst amongst
the 4,973 who
had been subject to the process
of vaccination, in only 567 instances had. the
disease proved fatal, giving a mortality of but
11.40. A considerable number had undergone
the process of re-vaccination, but without
effect, and the doctors had informed them that
as they were not susceptible to the vaccina-
tion, they had no fear of taking the small-pox'.
The presence of these -persons in the hospital
was a sufficient proof of the fallacy of this
doctrine, one inculcated evert. yet by ,many
members of the pro feision.

Lord de Maulay's non-attendance before
Mr. Registrar repys has again necessitated
an adjournment ot the discussion of several
questions interesting to the sporting World.
They turn on claims arising out of betting
transactions, which have been rejected by the
trustee of the' estate. The Registrar declined
to grant any order without the evidence of the
bankrupt.

Prince Arthur has returned to town from
his Liverpool trip. Before leaving the Mersey,
he paid a visit to the Sailors' Home, and the
last incident in his visit was a demonstration
which the Liverpool brokers made in his
honour on his casual appearance near the
Stock Exchange.

At the Anti-Income Tax Conference most
of the denunciation was done by proxy. Mr.
Sheridan, M.P., and the Rev. Canon Trevor
furnished papers to be read. A Mr. Hickling,
who accepted the full responsibility of his own
opinions unfolded a scheme for raising over
nine millions sterling from property at present
untaxed. Coal, ships, steamers, steam-engines,
railway and joint-stock capital were the virgin
soil he recommended to have cultivated.
revision of the probate duty and an exteilsion
of the house duty to houses under £2O rental
were relied upon to complete Hickling's sub-
stitute for the income-tax.

In giving a formal opinion of the right,
which had been questioned, of a Mr. Purcell, a
Moravian, to hold a fellowship in Trinity
College, Dublin, Mr. Dowse and Mr. Ball have
decided that such a right has always existed,
and that the College authorities have been in
error in exacting membership of the Church
of England as the condition of holding a
fellowship.

In a case which came before the Clerkenwell
police magistrate on Saturdayevidence was given
of a man having sold his wife for a sovereign.
One of the witnesses stated that there was a
"regular bargain" between the husband and
the purchaser, who had since quarrelled about
the woman, and the matter had ended in an
alleged assault., in which the husband was the
prosecutor. Mr. Barker described tho conduct
of all concerned as disgraceful, and dismissed
the complaint.

Whitsuntide charges have been fairly
numerous at the police-courts, though not
sarious. At Marylebone there were between
sixty and seventy, while at Clerkenwell the
total was as low as twenty-five.

• At the Middlesex Sessions the Metropolitan
Railway Company obtained convictions against
all the three pickpockets who were so neatly
detected by the company's officials at South
Kensington. Morrison, against whom previous
convictions were recorded, received seven
years' penal servitude ; Heaton and Harrison
twelve mouths' imprisonment. On the same
occasion Sir William Bodkin condemned to
seven years' compulsory retirement a French-
man who had been looting furnished lodgings
—in one case to the extent of .£3O. A. virago
from the House of Detention was sentenced
to twelve months' imprisonment for assaulting
a female warder with a tin pannikin in testi-
mony of her disapproval of short rations.

Professor Fawcett, M.P., who, together with
Mr. Bruce, Mr. Glyn, Mr. Lefevre, &a., has
been visiting Mr. Bass, M.P., at Glen Tulchan,
has been actively engaged in salmon fishing on
the Spey. The hon. gentleman, who wades
into the deepest and swiftest parts of the
stream, has been rewarded by the capture of
several fine salmon, one of them weighing
upwards of twenty pounds.

Forty-five of a crew arc said to have been
drowned by the wreck of a fishing brig oft the
coast of Labrador.

•
Two women have attempted to commit
suioideby throwing themselves into the Thames
but each was rescued.

• Earl Cathcart has been elected President of
the Royal Agricultural Society for the ensuing
year. At the half-yearly meeting, which was
held on Wednesday, the report stated that the
total number of members in the society was
now 5,766. This ye ir's annual meeting will
be held at Cardiff, while the 1873 gathering is
to take place at Hull.

The Captain Memorial Fund Committee,
which was established at Portsmouth, has re-
solved to pce a painted window in West-
winker Abbey, commemorative of the terrible
disaster off Cape Finisterre on the night or the
6th September,'l67o. The proposal has been
sanctioned by Dean Stanley.

During the week ending Saturday, the 18th
inst.,. 5,213 births and 3,314 deaths were
registered in London and twenty other large
cities and towns of the United Kingdom. The
rnortlitity from all causes in these towns was
at the rate of 23 deaths annually to every
1,030 persons estimated to be living. In
Edinburgh the annual rate of mortality Was
33 per 1,000 persons living, iu Glasgow 30
per 1,000, and in Dublin 29.

A. "foo 1 " between two pleasure boats off
Eelpie isliul, near Twickenham, has resulted
in the drowning of lour young men. The
survivors bt.tte that in an altercation which
followed the collision one boat was upset,
and those in he other boat capsized themselves
in uttemptH; to save their friends.

We are glad to be able to announce tpe
safe accouchement of Mrs. Bates, nee Anna
Swann, the Nova Scotian giantess. The
ohild, which was a girl, was born dead. It
was of enormous size—measured 28 inches
from crown to heel, and weighed •181bs. It
bore a strong resemblance to its mother in
facial lineaments, and also in eertaia physical
peculiarities.—L and and Water.

The Licensed Victuallers' Parliaments,ry
Committee on Wednesday passed a resolution
urging the importance of uniformity in the
hours of closing on week-days in the metro-
polis and in provincial towns with more than
10,000 inhabitants. The necessity of amonding
the Government Bill with respect to the iSsue
of grocers' licenses was also pointed out.

0n Wednesday the Congress of Law
Students at Birmingham passed a resolution,
condemning the present system of examination
as carried out by the Incorporated Law So-
ciety, and suggesting some alterations in the
mode of procedure.

The British and Foreign Unitarian Associa-
tion has, by a large majority, liaised a resolu-
tion declaring that the Education Act of 1870
contains provisions which violate the principles
of religious equality.

A collision occurred in the Waterloo Station
on Monday which caused only slight injury,
but produced considerable excitement aranng
the holiday-seekers who were crowding the t.
platform at the time.

In the action brought by Mr. Hepworth
Dixon against the Pall Mall Gazelle, the
Court of Common Pleas • have granted a rule
calling upon the defendant, Mr. Smith, t
show cause why
,certain interrogatories should
not be directed to him, which asked him, in,
'effect, to state whether he was or not pro.
prietor of that paper.

The objection to Inveresk as the winner cf
the Chester Cup has been overruled by the
&wards of the Jockey Club.

A woman named Cullen was on. Wednesday
convicted at the Middlesex Sessions of having
stolen a child three years old. She was
sentenced to two years' imprisonment with
hard labour, but begged hard for a longer
term of penal servitude, "as it would keep her,
from the drink." The judge,- however, de-
clined to grant her request.

At the Worship-street Police-court on
Wednesday an omnibus conductor, named
Taylor, was fined £5, with the alternative of
two months' imprisonment, for having been in
unlawful possession of a gold watch, the
property ot the Duchess of Cleveland.

A new Liberal club was inaugurated at
Liverpool on Wednesday night, whew an ad-
dress upon the past work and future prospects
of the Liberal party was delivered by, Mr. G.
0. Trevelyan, M.P.- The hon. gentleman be-
lieved that, notwithstanding the criticism's
which had been passed upon the leadership of
Mr. Gladstone, every division list showed that
the men
,who instinctively shared -the feelings
of the great bulk of the Liberal party were
determined to see the Government through their
present difficulties. As to the future; he was
hopeful that good sense and mutual good feel-
ing might complete the reconciliation betweeri
the different sections of the party. Let the
Government show that they have a compre-
hensive educational policy, and old associa-

SATURDAY, MAY 25, 1872.

HORSEWHIPPING A LABOURER.

WE are not disposed to doubt the oft-re-
peated assertion that a great deal of kindness
towards their labourers exists amongst the
farmers. It would be a contradiction of what
is universally admitted as to the kindness and
generosity of Englishmen generally, to sup-
pose that in suoh relation much mutual kind-
ness of feeling did not exist. But it would
be against all experience at the same time not
to admit that the extreme poverty, the gross
ignorance, the general degradation and
squalor, and the utter dependance of the men
did not breed in the minds of farmers indif-
ference and contempt for those whose very
presence is so frequently a burden, and nearly
always a reproach. It is net in the nature of
things that the farmer should regard the
labourer who works for insufficient pay, and
who ekes out his poor weekly reward. with
" perquisites " and poor rates, as a man to be
treated_ with the respect which independent
working men demand and receive. The
absolute conditions of slavery have gone, but
the mark of the slave's collar is yet on the
labourer's neck.
" Gurth, the son of Beowulf,
• Saxon Cedric 's thrall,"
can now at least call himself a freeman with-
out being "amerced in the sum of a mark "for
the offence as in the time of HENRY 11.
Still he is not out of danger, as Bonrisn
,
the Oxfordshire labourer, found out the other
day.
This audacious man had, it seems, attended a
labourers' meeting, and according to his master
(Mr. GARRETT) had sought to make his fellow
labourers dissatisfied with their condition.
For this offence Mr. GARRETT horsewhipped
him, as the account states, till he became ex-
hausted. Naturally enough, BODFISII sought
the protection of the law; and after being sent
by the superintendent of the police at Banbury
to Mr. Nona's, a magistrate for the oounty,
found out that this worthy gentleman was
very anxious that the offence should be con-
doned rather than punished. Ho declined to
grant the summons without seeing the gentle-
man who had plied the horsewhip, and when
these worthies met, three or four pounds was
settled as the sum to be paid. This sum was
refused by BODEISII, BO that a further bid will
have to be made, or the law will kayo to take

its course, even at the risk of such perversion
of its spirit as may exist amongst the county
magistrates of Oxfordshire.

How far the spirit which led to this horse-
whipping of poor BODFISH may exist in the
country amongst our farmers we cannot pre-
tend to say, but we can have no hesitation ia
declaring it to be dangerous in the last degree.
We may add also our inability to decide how
far a disposition to palter with justice may
prevail. But if words of ours can have any
effect on such persons, we would ask them
seriously and earnestly not to provoke retalia-
tions by violence, and not to shake the faith
of the people in the justice of the law, or th!
impartiality of its administration. ThL
labourers should join unions is, no doubt, ex.-
ceedingly provoking. That they should be
dissatisfied with their condition, and seek for
higher wages, does appear on the . face of it a
very monstrous iniquity. But it must not be,
forgotten that we live in, strange times, and
must expect to see very strange things, and as
law-breaking by violence is a most dangerous
game for our respectable classes to indulge in, •
they will be wise if they endeavour to control
their tempers and refrain from it.
The labourers should at any rate be careful
not to follow this evil example. By means of
a cheap and free press, public opinion will
control these men without violent retaliations.
Peace and order are amongst the best allies
of the labourers. They must not permit any-
one to provoke them to violence. Let what
will be said, the game is in their hands if they
play it judiciously and in a thoroughly law-
abiding spirit. Their wages will have to he
advanced, and their general comfort increased.
Let them get thought and determination into
their minds. Let them form their unions
and get strength; a common understanding,
common demands, and united action, and
nothing can withstand them. Life and hope
are just beginning to stir them, and if they
work with resolution and patience " GURTII
the son of BEowtrur," will stand in the presence
of Saxon Crome erect, independent and capa-
ble of making his arrangements as to wages
and other requirements in a spirit of manly
independence suitable to his position as a freo
worker.

The following is a bad beginning :

A meeting of agricultural labourers, at which
about one thousand were present, was held on
Tuesday at 'fairley, a village in Huntingdonshire,
and ended in a serious riot between the labourers
and the farmers, and iq which the women engaged
on rarms, for the first time, came to the front in a
determined way.
A chairman being appointed from the men pre-
sent, Mr. Savage proceeded to address the
assembly, when a number of farmers, their sons
and friends, marched on to the green, having in
each hand bird-clapperi, and drowned the voice
of the speaker. The disturbance was pa-
tiently borne until the labourers had taken
the measure of the farmers present, when
a message was sent to them that they
had better leave the men alone, or it would fare
badly with them. The answer to this was a
renewal of the clapper din. As soon as speech
could be heard a stalwart labourer shouted " Nolls,
we can stand this no longer," and with one action
the " Nolls " made a furious charge on the
farmers. The young farmers stood the fight
bravely, many of the labourers not desiring to
hurt their masters; but the strangers tram the
other farms were not so mercifully disposed, and
the bird-clappers were most 'unsparingly used on
the heads' backs, and legs of the young and old
squires. Blood flowed freely on each side, when,
pressed by superior numbers and strength, the
farmers fled for their lives. They were chased,
thumped, and knocked down, from the green into
the town where another hand to hand fight took
place until the landlords of the public-houses and
the tradesmen came to their rescue.
The fight being over, the meeting again resumed,
when some of the men spoke more hotly than
before' and the contest appeared to have made
them determined not to accept the offer made by
many masters of 14s. a week, but to go in for
more.

The women who were engaged in the affray gave
their husbands some trouble to quiet them and pre-
vent a further attack on the farmers in their horao-
steads.
A number of men and women were enrolled,
and in the end the labourers dispersed peaceably,
refusing to go into public-houses by the advice of
the delegates, lest a further riot should occur.

THE SUPPLEMENTARY ARTICLE.
Oun people have been so anxious as to
whether or not they should procure the assent
of the American Government to the Supple-
mentary Article of the Washington Treaty,
that its probable effect in influencing the
future welfare of the confracting Parties
seems scarcely to have been taken iito
account.

No doubt the provisions it contains will
apply alike to both parties. But what we
desire to know is, whether both will be effected
by it in an equal degree. In the Alabama
raids the stake we played for was the carrying
trade of the United States. There was besides
a desire generally existing amongst our upper
and aristocratic classes that the Great Re-
public should go to pieces. Political considera-
tions promoted. this political prejudices
turned it into a passionate hope. If this
desire had been shared in by the working
people, it might have led to war. Instead of
being shared in it was strongly opposed, and,
therefore, no act was performed by which the
nation could be held committed to any
hostility towards America. But what was
a hostility of prejudice in our upper
classes existed as a hostility of interest in
our trading classes. Hence the Alabama
and its confreres, and the transference of the
carrying trade of the ocean from the American
to the British flag, and hence, as a consequence
enormous money gains to British speculators.
This offence, which originated chiefly in
commercial greed, has become a national affair,
and its settlement ,must necessarily have
serious national consequences. It is our duty
to forecast these that we may understand more
correctly the character of the proposed settle-
ment. The intention is to abolish for ever all
right of claim for indirect losses in the future.
Meaning such claims as those made recently
on us by the United States Government. Now,
in the future, if the risks to both nations through
war are to be the same, the bargain is a
very fair one. But is this the case? Are the
two nations in this respect on a level? Will
the forbearance of America be in anyway like
the forbearance we are likely to be called on
to practice? We think it may be said with
truth that America has got its first and last
great war over. It would. be dangerous to
prophesy on this subject. Nevertheless, at the
present moment it is difficult to see how
America can be drawn into any contest in
anyway resembling in magnitude that out of
which she has so recently come. In fact, it
may be centuries before another chance is pre-
sented to us of rendering ourselves amenable
to America for a repetition of our Alabama
deeds, so that in giving up all claim for in-
direct damages, the American Government is
abandoning very little.
Is this the case with us? Can we say

that the curse of war is as far from
us as from the great American Republic?
We cannot, by the appearance of things, or by
any known process of logic, say that such is
the ease. We are bound by treaty engage-
Monts in Europe, which at any moment may
drag us into some frightful continental em-
broilment. France preparing for general
armament. Germany, at any moment, ready
to take the field. Austria nursing herself in
auger in consequence of her recent disoom-
liture. Turkey swelling herself into the pro-
portions of a first•olass belligerent. Russia
looking on with the view of renewing her last
ineffectual attempt, and revenging her sore
humiliations. Italy anxious for strengthening
alliances. And Spain fermenting with an-
tagonistic principles and passions. England
cannot, if she would, cut herself off from the
rest of Europe. She has done much, and may
do much still to keep herself clear of the
quarrels of her neighbours; but the
cloud may gather over her head and
burst at any moment; and then how
will the supplementary conditions of the Wash-
ington Treaty operate? We do not know what
port the double of an Alabama may issue
from. The American Government will, no
doubt, be very friendly, but it will find it
difficult to watch such an extensive seaboard
as belongs to it. Besides, having done all that
can be reasonably expected or legally looked
for, such a dangerous craft may find its way
out on our ocean highways, and do immense
damage to the mercantile navy of Great
Britain. If we do not know where such a
vessel may come from, we know very well
where our carrying trade would go when she
made her appearance. And who would pocket
the profits arising from it. "The whirligig
of time brings round its revenges;" and
Why not to us as well as to others? It
Is Amoriott whioh is now giying up its bill

for indirect damages, but she is doing So
on conditions which will for ever prevent Us
from presenting one. We suggest this point
as rather perplexing, without at all pretending
to know how the matter can be mended. In-
deed we knoiv not what effect such a discussion
can have beyond filling us with Wonder at our
own folly in the Alabama blunder. Com-
mercial greed is a hard thing to control, and
perhaps Earl RUSSELL, under trying eircurn-
stinees did his best to control it. But he
ought we think, at the present moment, try
to hold his tongue. "The times have been,
that when the brains were out the man would
die." There is, however, a wonderful tenacity
of life in the present day in some of our
statesmen.

EXPATRIATED COSIMUNISTS.

ON reading the accounts which have ap-
peared in the Daily Newe of the expatriated
communists, the first desire that arises is to do
something for their relief. Seldom has a more
pitiable tale been told, and more seldom still
has any Government, however cruel in dealing
with political delinquents, exceeded that of
H. Trims in the meanness and malignity of
its cruelty. The men who were indiscrimi-
nately shot down when the Versailles troops
entered Paris were mercifully used. Their
shrift was short—their suffering soon over.
A. few ball-cartridges, sharp death aptly, a
-common grave, and then a little 'hurried
scavenging to cleanse away the bloo&stains,
and all was over.

Not so with those taken prisoners. Long
months of weary imprisonment, hunger, cold,
misery in every form; a trial when it came,
which travestied justice, condemnation, and
deportation. Cayenne is too far off. The
expense of sending the victims there would be
too much, so they are paid for by the police,
and shipped for England without food, money,
or other necessaries. In this state the poor
wretches have to beg their way to London,
subsisting on charity, and in. London, though
their misery is to some extent alienated, we
see by Mr. ROBINSON'S letter in the Daily
News, how hard their fate is.
The immense drag net by which these people
were swept into the prisons of M. TRIERS, and
the mock trials they after wards underwent,
furnish no proof of guilt; and this being the
case, have not all men a right to ask, why
these horrible oruelties are practised?
As a matter of course, the English people
will do their duty, and, by subscribing, procure
food for those poor fellows ; but the question
will still remain to be answered, Why, in the
19th century? Why, for political offences, these
shocking barbarities are permitted? If these
men are as vile as the French Government
proclaims them, M. TRIERS is committing a
gross offence in turning them loose on our
shores, an offence for which our Govern-
ment should hold him strietly accountable.
But if they are not suoh wretches as they have
been stated to be, if they are honest working
men brought accidentally under the rigour of
military law by the exceptional and trying
circumstances of their country, then M. TRIERS
and his Government, and their police, are
committing an outrage against humanity
which must cover them for ever with infamy
in the eyes of the world.

PARTIES IN THE FRENCH ASSEMBLY.

SOME fine eloquence has been expended in
the National Assembly of France hi thrice
slaying the slain. Some days beforeWhitsuntide
the Duke of ATTDIFFRET-PA.SQUIER let off a
splendid piece of oratorical firework against the
Empire. Never was such a speech heard before;
not, at least, in the Parliament at Versailles.
It was spoken of as having crushed. the hopes
of the Bonapartists with as much enthusiasm
as if, till• the DUKE had spoken, those hopes
were on the point of passing from blossom into
fruit. With equal confidence it was predicted
of this display of rhetoric that it would make
the Legislative and Executive Powers embrace
each other in a clasp that nothing would be
able to sever. Not, however, to disparage the
effort, as though it were talk without practical
purport and effect, the noble speaker gave, in
a clear and compact form, the results of a long
inquiry before three-score investigators who
examined some two thousand documents,
Ow main result being that under the Empire

the country was robbed to an extent almost
beyond the power of arithmetic to set in figures.
At auy rate, this great hit, made by a high
member of the old nobility, had success enough
to call out the most renowned spokesman of the
subverted rule.. Whitsuntide was not over
when M. ROUITER caused it to be known that

he would take the tribune against this formid-
able Duke; and, on Tuesday accordingly, he
spoke for three long hours in a Chamber
crammed beyond precedent. The Duke had
promised not to ba political, ye f had been little
else; he would avoid polities altogether, and keep
close to contracts and matters of account.
Imagine the dreariness of three long hours
devoted to subjects so dry. But the eniotions
of the tribune, said the Imperialist orator,
were not always wholesome, and nothing was
less patriotic than a barren agitation. This
uncertain sentence called forth a single cheer,
the soleness of which, perhaps, the more
clearly shows how equivocal the sounding
nothing was. When the whole speech comes
to be reprinted, we shall better see whether it
contained anything to which M. TRIERS need
give himself the trouble of replying. In
closing, M. RoruEn made a cunning appeal
to the country party while seeming to
apostrophise one of their chief hates. M.
Ga.atnErra, he remarked, had told them, that
the alternatiVe lay betwixt dissolution of that
Assembly and dissolution of the State; but
that Assembly's task was to restore order and
reinstate security, and its premature dissolu-
tion would be quickly followed by that of
their country. But again there , was but a
• single cheer, showing that OTIIELLo'S occupa-
tion is indeed gone.
On the following day, the substantial por-
tions of M. RornEn's long sOech called up
the Duke of AUDIFFRET-PASQUIER, who
achieved a second Parliamentary success. M.
RatatEn had defended Count Paunac's con-
tracts, on the ground of pressure put upon
him by public opinion to get arms quickly.
M. TRIERS himself was among the most
clamorous. The COUNT had been blamed for
treating with middle men in England; but he
could not do otherwise. The laws of neutrality
prevented him from treating directly. Prussia
would never have tolerated the exportation of
arms from England unless through inter-
mediate agents. As to the million franca
advanced to the contractor CIIOLLET, it was
necessary, in the bad state of the credit of
France, in order to get arms at all, and he
endorsed the responsibility of the contract. To
these and other similar defences set up, the
Duke replied in detail, and in a tone
severely denunciatory of the subverted
Empire. The real question, he said, was,
why was not the Empire ready for war, con-
sidering the credits voted, and the assurances
repeatedly given of the satisfactory state of
the armaments.. Let the Empire restore to
Franco her legions, her glory, and her pro-
vinces. This apostrophe caused passionate
applause through the House; and the orator
concluded with a warm eulogy of the patriot-
ism, energy, and ability of M. THIERS. M.
Rorunn maintained, in rejpinder, the accuracy
of his statements. He then attacked the
contracts made by M. GADIBETTA, M. ROURER
was frequently interrupted from all parts of
the Chamber, and though he spoke for two
hours, made no reply to the principal attacks
of the Duke, and attempted no defence of the
Empire, never mentioning the Emperor's
name, M. atunErra, defended his contracts,
demanded inquiry, and confidently awaited
the result. The Assembly formally adopted
an order of the day, proposed by the Duo de
BROGLIE, and accepted by the leaders of 41
parties :—" The Assembly, confiding in the
exertions of the Committee, and maintaining
its resolutions to prosecute all persons respon-

Bible, whether before or afthr the 4th o:

September, passes to the order of the day."
The voting was 692 ayes, and no noes. M.
TIIEIRS was present, and found no occasion
,to
break silence.

THE MANCHESTER 'UNITY OF ODD-
FELLOWS.

TILE annual moveable committee of the
Manchester Unity of Odd-Fellows has been
meeting at Lancaster. Grand-Master GINN-,
attorney, of St, Ives, Hunts, presided. The
facts of the report were encouraging, No

fewer than 35,260 members had been admitted
showing, a nett increase. of 15,584, against
8,475 in 1870. Of the newly initiated, .22,391 ,
were under twenty-five years .of, age.. Sur-
prise was, expressed that ,no report had been
issued by the, Friendly Societies' Commission,'
although, so far back as 'November, 1870, a
deputation from the Unity was examined.
The assets and liabilities of the Macclesfield
district, which
,last year applied for relief,
showed a . deficiency of £2,805 12s. Gd. The
funds possessed by three lodges, with 410
members, only 'amounted to .£1,040 Is., whilst'
two, with 119 members and 21 district MM.
bers, had no funds whatever.
,The payments
of members admitted since' 1853 had been
adequate for the benefits, but the money
,had
gone to meet former liabilities. The total
deficiency was equal to a rise of more than one- ,
third in the contributions of all members.,
This valuation, and that of the Manchester
district, showed the utter inadequacy of any
gift the Annual Moveable Committee could
make, the deficiency in interest alone being
over £BO per annum. Returns have been ob-
tained, preparatory to a valuation of all lodges
in. the United' Kingdom, but the work could
not be completed in time; and. the question
how the poorer districts should be dealt' with
Must stand over., The directors
,during the
' year declined to allow any lodges to appro.,
priate surplus capital. The quinquennial
ret urns to December showed au increasing in-
tensity of sickness, not alarming, yet sufficient.
to suggest caution. Thantanagentent OXpialSeS
last year were .£1,091, a decrease of £118; the
profits from all sources were £1,020, an ;increase
of £34. . • ,

• The Hon. LYULPIE STANLEY, Assistant Com-
missioner of the Friendly Societies Commission,
attended the second day's sitting, at which the
separation of districts, unless good grounds
could be shown, was condemned. A penny
levy was ordered throughout the Unity to
defray the expenses of the valuation; and the
meeting endorsed the action in refusing to
allow surplus capital to be appropriated by
lodges. At the third day's sitting, an altera-
tion was made in the mode of electing, by
which in future printed lists of the candidates
will be distributed, and tho voting taken by
papers instead of show of hands. A proposal
to disqualify for twelve months. the director
longest on the board, in favour, of new blood
being infused, was rejected by a hundred and
thirty-eight votes to twenty. A proposition
for a greater levy than a shilling for the sup-
port of district members was defeated. , The
meeting decided not to allow lodges to break
up without consent of district and board of
directors.

began with less than fifty labourers; in two
months, it has resulted in a union of a
thousand times that number. Among other
counties, it has found a source of new strength
in Buckinghamshire. If, as seems likely,
.it
should eventually take 'the form of a good
understanding betvveen the farmer and the
labourer, the source of improvement will be
as evident and as generally acknowledged
as the need of it is felt and palpable.
What, in the meantime, can be plainer,
than that, if the farmer is made to
increase the labourer's wages, he must have
rent so adjusted as to relieve the pressure upon
himself? The landlords have an alternative
in their hands: if, for example, they should
allot to each hand half an acre for cultivation
on his own account, that would he equivalent
to something like an increase of thirty-three
per cent, in his wages. Mr. DISRA.ELT, after
his own fashion, endeavoured to exempt the
county whieli he represents from the,odium of
oppressing the peasantry; but the endeavour
is vain in the face of facts. What can he
made of such instances as that of a man
with a wife and ten children, or half the
number, earning but thirteen shillings, in-
cluding a Sunday's labour? Who can be
surprised that,, if to house, feed, and, clothe
his family, he should often continue his work
from morning to afternoon without a dinner.
Were there more Canons GIIIDIXSTONE, and
fewer country parsons of another sort„ qua,
tiOnti of this nature might be muoh sooner and

better settled. The other day this benevolent
clergyman took his leave of Halberton, in
Devonshire, in a farewell address to the
assembled labourers of the parish. When he
entered the village, the miserable state of the
people quite depressed him, from the great
contrast presented to what he had seen in the
North. Ho at once resolved to do what he
could to relieve them. The way that he
found most practicable was to send superfluous
bands to counties where there was a demand
for labour at higher wages. From Halberton
and its vicinity, ho had thus transferred four
hundred labourers to Yorkshire and the North,
a migration from nine shillings a week in
Devonshire to rather more than twice
the sum at the other end of the king-
dom. Thus, while he sent the surplus to
places whieh appeared to them like the Gar-
den of Eden in comparison, he converted the
natural paradise left bohind into a more goodly
-heritage in behalf of those who remained on
the spot, because, in proportion as the supply
of labour was thinned, wages must necessarily
rise. Another shilling had been added by the
farmers just before the CA.Norf went away. In
this last sermon, the reverend gentleman
strongly preached the duty and advantage of
"union." "Unless united they would never
raise wages to what they ought to be, nor
maintain the rise. By union they would get
the whole in current coin, instead of part in
liquor. Nothing was so degrading in his mind
as that the labourer should be dictated to as
to how he should receive his wages. By being
united, too, they would obtain better houses
for themselves. It was not the farmer's fault
that their houses were so bad. They must
unite against the landowners in this question:
Some houses were not fit for cattle, much loss
for Christian men and, women. Parliament
wished the country to be a self-governing one,
and this being the case, every man who owned
a rateable cottage should have a right to vote.
But did a labourer dare go to a vestry and
take part in the election of a waywarden, of a
guardian, or of a member of a school board?
Why not? Because they wore afraid of their
masters. But, if they were united, they could
with a bold face demand to vote as well
as their masters." Bravo ! Canon OIRDLE-
STONE.

THE ADVANCE OF BRITISH LABOUR.
[CommuneAnn.]
How encouraging it must be to those that
take a pleasure in upholding the cause of the
industrious part of the British community.
Every trade, from the most lucrative to the
least productive kind of labour, seems to have
received reanimation, and arisen from the
usual round of unchangeable tyranny and
oppression. From the highest scientifie
engineer to the most ill-paid agricultural
labourer, a (*Anse has, or is is about, to take
place. The rapid and effeetive manner in
which the working-classes are advancing is
seen more plainly in every impression of the
BEE-HIVE. As though the Education Ad,
which is in force for the children of this gene-
ration, had brought with it a mirror of what
is right for the good of the poor of more
mature years, and a degree of determination
to rise to a different position, before their
better educated children. are old enough to see
the shameful and degraded manner in which
they have been compelled to live. It has,
indeed, been a poor life, with a definite pros-
pect of nothing bettor; from children of
eleven or thirteen have they been learnt to
toil on, with just sufficient to keep body and
soul together; year after year with no im-
provement, and no richer than when they
first began the dull routine of life.
Nay, they are still worse, without a pros-
pot of becoming better, They are married,
and coftpelled to maintain a wife and family
out of what seemed to be a marvel to keep
life in tlemselves.

"Begin their life a ragged youth,
And find a pauper's grave.' .
And yet, what was the lesson of those that
reaped all the benefit, what was the encourage-
ment given by the rich to their more unfor-
tunate fellow-beings? They simply said
honesty, industry, and economy must un-
doubtedly flourish. Like some of our reverend
pastors, if a poor balf-ntarved beggar asks for

a piece of bread to satisfy his hunger they
offer him a tract.

But now the curtain is being drawn up,
and the mazy scenery is about to be dashed
aside, and we soon shall be able to see
"behind the scenes." The rich capitalist will
still reign king of his own little dominion,
but his industrious servitor will no longer be
dependant upon his " generosity " alone. ,He
will not permit those servile underlings to
treat him even worse than his master; and
neither will he allow himself to be held down
by a fear of his master's displeasure, or his
own dismissal.

The tyranny and oppression that has been
used towards the working classes has only
brought things to a successful issue somewhat
earlier than it otherwise would have done,
and even a little sooner than was anticipated.
The tall-talking capitalist sees his power of
oppression fade away, and he will yet find
that such management as Mr. JOHN SMEDLEY'S
will not only bring the greatest credit that
master can win, but will be preduetive of the
best results both to himself and business.

If a poor man has no right to higher wages
that he may improve himself, what more right
has a capitalist worth £2,000 to be allowed
to continue his business until he is worth
£20,000, when the poor man does all the
work, lives on the least, and is no better off
than when he first began.
That the male part of the working classes
are advancing with rapid strides is an un-
doubted fact; and that the females have as
great a right to improvement, is also beyond
question. Indeed, they have been sadly
neglected too long already, and it behoves
every one of us to give them our support in
every possible way to accomplish that which
it would be injustice on our part to leave
them to struggle for themselves.

MIDDLE-CLASS FLUNKEYISII.

[CONTRIBUTED.]
TRE last number of the Nation (New York
contains some remarks on the recent excite-
ment regarding the Marquis of BUTE'S wed-
ding, which are not wholly undeserved, and
which it may, therefore, not be amiss to re-
produce. A writer in that journal observes
that at that time a large part of the Daily
Telegraph was occupied with glaring descrip-
tions of the extraordinary manifestations of
delight exhibited by a large population in
England, Wales, and Scotland; of parties of
London tradesmen dining together in a rap-
turous state of mind, making speeches, corn-
posipg addresses, and overflowing through all
the established channels of enthusiasm; of
the inhabitants of a Welsh sea-port town
turning out into the streets in a condition of
excitement which the pen of the reporter
utterly fails to describe; and of the sturdy
farmers in Scotland. rivalling the warmth of
their-More excitable southern fellew-country-
men, What was the cause of this
passionate emotion? If the Telegraph be
right, even the recovery of the Prince of
WALES, or the speech-making, of Mr.
DISUAELI at Manchester, did not so stir the
popular bosom. Well, if the truth must be
told, it was that a young gentleman was about
to be married. That happens, it may, be said,
every day; but this young gentleman was a
marquis. Even so, the marriage of a marquis,
though doubgess calculated to convey a thrill
of sympathetic joy to the plebeian breast, is not
a quite unprecedented phenomenon. This
young marquis, mereover, had committed the
one fault to which the middle-class English-
man has—and, in my private opinion, with
much justice—the heartiest aversion; he was
A pervert to Popery, ana had been chiefly dis-
tinguishing himself by presenting a capful
of jewellery (I don't know whether I am
precisely right in the nature of the present)
to poor old Pto Noxo.
What, then, was the amazing merit which
atoned for this enormity, and. made the mar-
riage of the marquis an event to be com-
memorated with as much bell-ringing, speech-
making, address•delivering, as many special
trains, and. as many columns in the Daily
Telegraph, as would suffice to celebrate a
national victory? Simply this: that the
Marquis of BtrrE is about the richest 'man in
England. Ile almost rivals our excellent

friend LOTIILIR ; and. even Popery, which is
detestable in an Ordinary form, gains a kind
of aristocratic grace, which makes it rather
ornamental than otherwise, when accompanied
by vast rentals, sumptuous palaces, and an
indefinite amount of cash balances. The wor-
ship of the dollar is, I believe, known to
exist occasionally in the United States.
I will not ask whether the combination of this
peculiar cultus with the worship of rank makes
it more or less respectable . . . whilst
the aristocracy excites such keen emotions in
the breast of the British JEsmEs, it doe i not
seem as if the ballot would destroy its power.
The feeling is too deeply seated and' too
evidently unaffected. Luckily, there are
limits beyond which the mob religion becomes
powerless, and feelings which on occasion can
get the better of it. For the present, however,
I must lay down my pen, lest I should be

hurried into some remarks not suitable to the
respect with which every, true Briton should
regard. the peerage of his country.

articles.title: IRONWORKERS' CONFERENCE.
articles.text:
THE IRONWORKERS' CONFERENCE.

THE delegates representing fifty thousand
ironworkers in all parts of the kingdom have
held their conference at Sheffield. The object
was to extend the association to , North
Staffordshire and East Worcestershire, as
well as to the iron districts of the Midland
Counties, by amalgamating all into one
general union. This accomplished, all claims
for an advance by workmen, with all reduc-
tions proposed by masters, arc to go before the
General Council, and a uniform policy for the
whole country is to be followed. The Union
is to comprise all men connected with the trade
in any of its departments.

THE WEATHER AND THE 'FIELDS.
AGRICULTURAL prospbcts may now, perhaps,
be spoken of with more approach to certainty
than while cold rains were falling and cold
winds blowing, and even night frosts biting.
Wheat prices had begun to move upwards.
The new plant, however, is strong, and looks
vigorous; and, in the south, the ear will soon
be shooting, especially if the fine weather
now setting in be uninterrupted. As far north
as Yorkshire, the absence of frosts is spoken
of as leading to a manifest improvement in all
the crops, which have assumed an appearance
decidedly more healthy. In short, under the
rays of an unclouded sun and with light
breezes of warmed air, there will be a rapid
development of everything well rooted in the
saturated soil, as the abundance of grain in
seedland, meadow, and pasture verdantly
shows. The downpour of Friday and Satur-
day in last week seems to have beeü the fare-
well of the Cold rains.

articles.text:
LAWS.

At a meeting of the Labour Representation
League, held on Friday evening, Mr. R. Marsden
Latham, the president, in the chair, the report just
issued by the select parliamentary committee on
the patent laws was discussed. Much dissatis-
faction was expressed with the report and at the
fact that members of the working classes had not
been called to give evidence before the Committee,
the constitution of which body was objected to on
the ground that its composition consisted two-thirds
of manufacturers and parties representing interests
antagonistic to those of inventors. It was also
urged that a fair and complete inquiry into so im-
portant a subject as the patent laws could only be
satisfactorily effected by a Royal commission
representing all the interests in the community,
and steps wore ordered to be taken with the view
of ensuring an exhaustive inquiry into the whole
subject by that means. It was also agreed that a
deputation should wait upon the council of the
Inventors' Institute in order to obtain their aid
and co-operation in the matter; and the following
resolution, proposed by Mr. Thomas Mottershead,
and seconded by Mr. Samuel Brighty, was carried
unanimously :—" That the recommendations of the
select Committee of the House of Commons on the
Patent Laws are by no means likely to benefit the
most numerous class of inventors, namely, the
artisans; and, if carried into effect, would render
the obtaining of a patent more difficult, climber-
some, and expensive than at present. Moreover,
the committee's recommendations do not provide,
what the generality of inventors stand mainly in
need of, namely, an assimilation as fat' as practie-
able, of the laws affecting inveation-right to those
of copyright, and especially increased facilities for
the obtaining by inventors of a valid property in
their own inventions at a reasonable cost, as is now
advantageously done in Belgium, France, and other
countries whose patent laws aro in arum* of
those of this country,"

TRADES INTELLIGENCE

LONDON.

THE HAILERS AND THE B.IIOKII ACT.

A numerously attenied meeting of master and
journeymen bakers, connected with the West-end
trade, was held on Saturday last at Seyntour-hall,
Seymour-street, Portman-square, Mr. Bonthron, of
Regent-street, in the chair, for the purpose of
protesting against the provisions of the Smoke
Nuisance Act being applied to the baking trade.
The chairman, in opening the proceedings, said,
had members of Parliament known anything
about bakers' ovens he felt certain bakers would
not have been subjected. to the provisions of the
Smoke Nuisance Act. A nuisance was a thing
that annoyed and offended, but the smoke from a
baker's oven was a thing that had to be looked for
before it could be discovered,

Mr. Ingles, a master, moved the following row"
lution :—" That this meeting, while admitting the
soundness of the principle of the Smoke Nuisanee
Act, is of opinion that the baking trade, ought
never. to have been included within its provisions,
inasmuch as it does not constitute a nuisance; ana
secondly, that its conditions are wholly dissimilar
to those of all others enumerated in the Act."
Mr. Scotland, a foreman, seconded the resolution
Mr. Thomson and Mr. Ward, journeymen, sup-
ported the resolution, which was adopted.
Mr. Linscott, a master, moved the following,
resolution :—" That the baking trade having
found, after nearly twenty years' coAly experi-
ence, that it is utterly impossible for its members
to comply with the Act, this meeting regards it as
a great oppression that they should be subject to
heavy fines or imprisonment for inability to cope
with scientific difficulties; it, therefore, calls upon ,
the Legislature to pass a Bill exempting the:
baking trade from the said Act."
Mr. M'Arthur, foreman, seconded, and Mr. ,
Webb, journeyman, supported the resolution,
which was carried.

The folloiving resolution was also adopted :
" That the Bill now before the House of Commons
under the oharge of Mr. John Locke receives the
Unqualified approval of the trade, as the best
measure that can meet its necessities." -
A petition to Parliament in favour of Mr.
Locke's Bill was agreed to, and the proceedings
closed with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

THE HOUSE PAINTERS AND THE NINE MUM

MOVEMENT.

For some time past the London house painters
have been quietly but effectually organising them-
selves to take active measures to secure, with other
branches of the building trades, the advantage of
shorter time of labour. In addition to this, many
non-society mon are subscribing handsomely to
enable tho Executive Committee to effectually
mirk out the work they have in hand. A series
of districts are arranged. The points to be sub-
mitted in the resolution i aro similiar:to those of
other trades.

articles.text:
DERBY.

THE STRIKE OF OPERATIVE SPINNERS.
• There is no sign of this difficulty
,coming to a
satisfactory termination. A few non-union men

came into the town and commeneed work, but on
being tad the spinners were on strike, they left
the place, their expenses being paid by the Silk
Throwers' Union.

The masters have emit round for some of the
men to return to work upon the same eonditions as
they went away; but the men—and most properly
too—refuse to resume work until their demands
are conceded. It appears that, the original de.
mand of the men, as at first presented, contained
a stipulation that they shall have time and quarter
time for all overtime, but in their if/tin:at:6a they
are willing to forego that part of the demand,
providing the masters will concede the advance of
two shillings. The men are in receipt of ten
shillings weekly from their union, and they appear
as determined to stay out as ever.
Your correspondent has been accused of being a
most partial and prejudiced writer because he has
not—like the rest of these public scribblers—taken
up the cause of the employers. But he can most
emphatically say, that he has never made a state-
ment or used a style of argument that he cannot,
and his not willing to upheld even now. if
has espoused the cause of thó men somewhat
warmly, it is because every provincial paper seems
to be SO against them, and also denies them that
fair play that is always found and appreciated ill
the columns of the Bas-Mvs. Perhaps I should
find some opposite Party to disapprove of my argu-
ments if it was not such a difficult matter to
publicly uphold a wrong cause.
FREDAZIO T. IL

, PERTH.
SEVEN TRADES' UNION' SIIOEMAKEIIS IMPRISONED

FOIL MOLESTING A WORKMAN.

On Thursday, before Sheriff Barclay, seven
shoemakers belonging to Perth, William Anderson,
Peter Blair, James Mill or Meiklejohn, Peter Smith,
Andrew Agnew, James M‘Gregor or Gregor, and
James Hobson, were charged, under the Summary
Procedure Act, with having molested or obstructed
two workman by "watching or besetting the
shop" in which they were emplOyed. The charge
was found proven as against one of the men who
were molested, and the facts as brought out in the
evidence appeared to have been these :—About the
beginning of March last a non-union man named
Peter Macfarlane get work in the shop of Mr.
Bannister, boot and shoemaker, Perth. The union
men objecting, to Macfarlane being allowed to
work, the latter (by the advice of his master, Mr.
Bannister,) joined the society "to keep peace with
the men." About the end of April a strike took
place for higher wages, and Macfarlane attended
a meeting of the society—the only one be ever
attended—at which he was fined 41 for " scab-
bing,"working at a reduced rate of wages.
Macfarlane denied the allegation, refused to pay
the pile, and left the union. During the strike he
continued at work, and the shop was watched
from the Ist May till the 9th—two men watching
at a time. It was stated, however, by Macfarlane
that these watches never at any time spoke to him,
or made any attempt at assault, ThQ Sheriff found
the charge of molestation proved, and sentenced
the accused to six days' imprisonment each. An
appeal was taken to the Justiciary Couit, and the
men were liberated on bail.

CAMBRIDGE.
THE BUILDERS' STRIKE.

I beg to forward you an account of our dispute
now pending in the building trade. Upwards of
400 operatives struck work on the Ist of May for
54 hours per week and 6d. per hour. Several
have left the town, and others obtained employ-
ment at firms who have conceded to our terms,
thereby reducing the strike list to about 200. I
am sorry to say there is but very little prospect of
its being settled yet. The employers are scouring
the country round for men. One employer has
obtained several old men out of the workhouse to
supply the place of the men on strike. They have
also brought the Criminal Law Amendment Act
into operation. One carpenter has been com-
mitted to fourteen days' for speaking to another
who had returned lo work. This is a most scan,
dalous law that over was passed in this country,
J. IL Coons.
Chairman of Nine Hours' League.

DUNDEE.
MEETING OF DOMESTIC SERVANTS.

The adjourned meeting of domestic servants
was held in the Thistle Hall on Friday evening,
for the purpose of drawing up rules and forming
an aarciation. The following rules were sub-
mitted:—

That this Association shall be called the Dundee
and District Domestic Servants' Association.
That the object of the Association shall be to
improve the/condition of the domestic servants by
rendering their work less burdensome and their
wages more liberal than at present.
That in the first instance servants shall have a
weekly; half .holiday, commencing at four o'clock,
and a free Sabbath every fortnight; but; while
insisting on these concessions, it is not to be
understood that necessary operations in the house,
which cannot, reasonably be left undone, shall not
be performed.
That, while it is impossible to arbitrarily settle
the working hours of servants, it is felt to be per-
fectly compatible with all demands that may be
made upon them thatl:they should have at their
absolute disposal three hours daily.
That engagements shall in future be made for a
period not exceeding one month, an arrangement
which has become imperative in consequence of
the annoyance which mistresses as well as servants
at present experience from the long interval which
elapses between the time when servants are com-
pelled to intimate their decision and the date of
the expiry of the engagement.

That fair and full latitude shall be accorded to
servants as to style of the apparel which they may
think it not improper for them to wear.

That, in order the More successfully:to secure
the general recognition of the changes indicated
above, each member of the Association shall
annually subscribe Is. to a fund which will be
devoted to the payment of salaries to the treasurer
and secretary for the time being, who will be
relieved of service, and thus be able to devote
their whole time and attention to the interests:of
the servants.

That it shall devolvo on those officials to keep
It registry at 04 office which will be established,

and that engagements shall in future be made
through this agency instead of through the regis-
tries now in existence.

BRISTOL. .
THE CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.

At Bristol, a meeting of employers and opera-
tive carpenters and joiners took place on Tuesday
last, Mr. Joseph Forster, chairman of the Local
Association, presiding. The notices issued by the
operatives were discussed at considerable length ;
the men who had asked for 7d. per hour were
offered 61d., the chairman also informing them
that the employers felt they could not withstand
giving the nine hears, but they most certainly felt
that the sum offered, 61(1., was as :much as they
ought to be expected to give, and as much as they
could really give, present contracts, being taken
into consideration. The operatives endeavoured
to show that they had only asked what they felt
they deserved, considering the general rise that
had taken place throughout the country, and in-
creased price of provisions. They could not, there-
fore, accept the terms offered by the employers,
but would communicate with their several lodges
and inform the employers the result. No answer
has as yet been received from the Masons' Society
to the proposals of the employers.

MAIDSTONE.
STRIKE OF CARPENTERS.

On Monday morning last the majority of the
carpenters in the employ of the builders of Maid-
stone abstained from commencing the week's work.
A meeting was held on Saturday evening last, and
it was announced that it was found to be impossible
to come to an amicable arrangement with the
employers, whereupon a resolution was passed that
the carpenters should "stand out," but that the
bricklayers should not do so at present. The
movement thus brought to a crisis has extended
over several months. The workmen first asked for
a reduction of working hours tool per week, with
a corresponding rise in wages—viz., from Gid, to
7d. per both.. To this the
,employers ,idemurred,
and offered 61d. per hour and 561 hours per week.
This proposal did not meet the views of the men,
who consented to meet the employers half-way in
money matter, but declined to exceed the nine
hours of work per day. Upon this point the split
has occurred.

LIVERPOOL.
TILE SAILORS AND THEIR WAGES.

A large meeting of the sailors of the port of
Liverpool was held on Monday, at which the re-
port of a committee was received recommending
the following rates of wages :—To the west as far
south as Orleans, considering the yellow fever,
£5 per month; to Cape Horn, £3 10s. ; the Pa-
cific (a healthy voyage), £3 Se.; the Mediter-
ranean (a short voyage), .£3 10s. ; coast of Africa,
£4; East Indies, Chinn, and Japan, .£3 55.; with
a month's advance in all cases. The present rates
for the respectivo voyages (with no advance) are
£4, £3, £3, £3 10s. for firemen, and £3 for
sailors; to the East Indies, &0., from £2 15s. to
£3, a general rise having recently taken place on
account of the scarcity of seamen. The burthon
of the sailors' complaints at the meeting was that
they cannot get into contact with the shipowners
to explain their grievances, not only as to wages,
but in respect to treatment on board ship ; and a
deputation was appointed by the meeting to await
upon the shipowners' and steamshipowners' as-
sociations to represent the case of the men. It is
understood that if the owners offar some advance
on the present rates, even if it is not equal to the
scale recommended by the committee, it will be
accepted.

articles.title: STAFFORDSHIRE POTTERIES.
articles.text:
STAFFORDSHIRE POTTERIES.

TILE JOINERS AND ARBITRATI ON.

In the Staffordshire Potteries Mr. 11. T. Devon.
port, who was appealed to as umpire upon the
demand of the carpenters and joiners for an in-
crease of wages and the adoption of the nine hours
system, has given his decision. An advance of
one farthing per hour in wages, making 6id., has
been conceded, and by a re-arrangement of the
hours, the nine hours period will practically be
worked during the winter months, the summer
hours remaining nearly the same as at present.

articles.title: HALIFAX.
articles.text:
HALIFAX.

THE CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.

In November last notice was given by the car-
penters and joiners of Halifax to their employers
that, at the end of six months, they should ask for
a reduction of their hours of labour from 521 t to
50 per week, and for an advance of wages from
275. to 28s. A deputation from the workmen
waited upon the employers on Tuesday evening
week, and on Saturday evening a largely-attended
4ieeting of the men was held at the Temperance
41411, Halifax, for the purpose of receiving their

report. Mr. James Cunningham presided, and the
deputation reported that the masters had made a
proposition to reduce the hours of labour by one-
and-a-half per day, the wages to remain as at pre-
sent; or they would give an advance of Is. per week,
the hours of labour to remain as at present. Th°
employers, had also hinted at the advisability of
submitting the question to arbitration. A long
discussion took place, after which it was unani-
mously resolved to reject the proposals of the
employers, and to adhere to their original pfoposi-

tion. It was also unanimously resolved not to
submit the question to arbitration. A committee
of seven was appointed to meet the masters, and
lay beforo:thom the decision of the meeting.

articles.title: SUNDERLAND. TILE NINE nouns MOVENIENT.
articles.text:
SUNDERLAND.
TILE NINE nouns MOVENIENT.

On Monday an outdoor demonstration was held
in Sunderland to celebrate the success of the
nine hours movement,:of which the engineers of
that town claim to be the pioneers. A procession
was formed in the morning in High-street,
headed by several brass bands, and marched to
the Town Moor, where resolutions were passed,
expressing confidenJe in the nine hours system,
and thanking the firms in Sunderland for the
readiness with which they met the demands of the
men. One of the speakers alluded to the great
amount of overtime which was now worked, and,
controverting the assertion that the fact proved
that the object of the men was virtually to obtain
an advance of wages, said if it was continued they
would have to oppose it, as they did the former
system of long hours. In the evening a dinner
was held, when
.Mr. Gourley, M.P., was present,
and responded to the toast of "The House of
Commons." He expressed his concurrence with
the now system, and [advocated the establishment
of technical colleges by the employers to teach the
workmen.

articles.title: NOTTINGHAM. DYER'S ASSOCIATION.
articles.text:
NOTTINGHAM.
DYER'S ASSOCIATION.

At a meeting held on Wednesday of the above
trade, the following resolution was passed
"That, having been made acquainted by our
esteemed fpresident, 11fr. John Nutt, that the
dyers of Bradford and district have expressed a
wish to appoint a delegation to pay a visit to our
society, with a view of promoting a fusion or an
amalgamation of the various existing societies of
our trade, we desire to avail ourselves of the pre-

To the Editor of the BuE-lltvE.

caution those who are about leaving the old country
to be very cautious of advertisements setting forth
in glowing colours, good workmen wanted at such

moans of inducing men who have had comfortable
homes to break up the seine (both in England and
America), and journey to this great land of pro-
mise, flowing with milk and honey. When
they have arrived it this fancied Elysium, they
have found all their pictured prospects blighted ;
whore plenty has been so graphically described in
their advertisement, a dearth of employm eat ex-
isted by the importation of a redundance of labour
by the ever-applied modus operandi of the em-

-verbatim extract from the letter just received from
Mr. Daniel F. Mulville., corresponding secretary
of the Operative Plasterers' Protective and Benevo-

pouring in upon us from all parts of Europe to

in England to beware of placing too much confl-
idence in the report abroad of high wages and

but the baso fabrication of wily capitalists to inun-
date Chicago with mechanics, and thus obtain
()heap labour. I would urge this more particularly

fortable homes." By inserting the above you will
greatly oblige yours, respectfully,
Cuts. WILLIAMS, General Secretary.

articles.title: TIIE LETTER CARRIERS.
articles.text:
TIIE LETTER CARRIERS.

The Lords of the Treasury have sanctioned an
increase in the wages of the Birmingham letter
carriers, such increase to take effect from the Ist
of May current. Under the old scale of payment
there existecl a supplementary class of town
carriers, in which the men had to remain for a
period of
,eight and nine months at a weekly
salary of 188. After this eight or nine months'
probation, these men wore draughted into an
established class, their wages beginning at 188. a
week, and rising 6d. a week annually until 235.
were reached. This referred to the town letter
carriers; but there was another class of men
called suburban carriers, whose wages commenced
at 18s. a week, and rose annually by sixpence a
week per annum until they reached 215., and
then stopped. Under the new arrangement which
has just received the sanction of the authorities,
the supplementary class of town letter carriers is
abolished, and the town men on entering the
service commence at 18s. a week, rising by Is. a
week annually to 235., and at the end of ten years'
service this 235. is increased to 255., which is the
maximum sum to be paid. The suburban carriers
begin at 183. a week, rising by is. a week every
year till 21s. is reached, where they stop. In
addition to this, the men in both classes receive
uniform clothing once every eight months,
gratuitous medical attendance, and after ton years'
service are entitled to a small pension. There is
another point which has been settled in favour of
the men, and that is, two-thirds of their weekly
pay is to be given them during illness, whereas
under the old system a uniform sum of Bs. weekly
was deducted from their salary during illness. I
will thus be seen that the Lords of the Treasury
have met the fiequent appeals of the men by the
adoption of a kind of middle course.

BOLTON.
TILE ENGINEERS AND FIREMEN.

On Saturday evening a numerous gathering of
engine drivers and firemen of stationary engines
was held in the Mechanics' Institute Lecture Hall,
Bolton, Mr. M. Dickinson in the chair. The chief
business of the meeting was the consideration of
the nine-hours question, and after a long discus-
sion, a resolution was passed that the following
circular should be sent to the employers of Bolton
and neighbourhood:—" The question of shortening
the hours of labour being paramount at the pre-
sent juncture, and 54 working hours:having been
generally accepted by the employers in the iron
trade as constituting a week, and pay for it as
such, we, the engine tenters and fireman em-
ployed in Bolton and district, consider we have
a just claim not to be exceptionally treated, inas-
much as we are classed with the same branch of
operatives. We are free to admit it to be imprac-
ticable under the present factory law to allow us
the privilege of shorter hours of labour, but we do
think that all hours made over and above 54 per
week ought to be paid as overtime. Hoping that
you will take this subject into consideration, and
comply with our request, we are, &c."
A committee was appointed to carry out the
objects of the meeting.

articles.title: MANCHESTER.
articles.text:
MANCHESTER.

PRESENTATION OF LlOO TO A. DISABLED:WOREMAN.
A meeting was held on Saturday in the Hulme
Town Ball, under the presidency of His Worship
the Mayor of Manchester, for the purpose of pre-
senting W. 11. Milburn, a member of the Amalga-
mated Society of Carpenters and Joiners, with a
purse containing £lOO accident benefit, he being
permanently disabled from following his employ-
ment.

The Mayor, in opening the proceedings of the
meeting, expressed himself much gratified that the
society to which the unfortunate individual be-
longed was in a position to band over to him the
handsome sum named. From what he had
gathered from the officials of the society, he under-
stood that Mr. Milburn, on leaving his employ-
ment on the Saturday afternoon when ho met With
the accident, was in a perfectly sober condition,
and that he was brutally assaulted by three
drunken men in Modlock -street, through which he
sustained such injuries as led to the total useless-
ness of his left arm to follow his ordinary occupa-
tion. Although not a total abstainer himself, he
was strongly in favour of temperance, and be
. would especially urge upon the present recipient
not to embark the sum he was about to receive in
' the same businesd.which bud indirectly led to his
present unfortunate position.
Mr. Prior, the general secretary of the Amalga-
mated Society of Carpenters and Joiners, in making
the presentation on behalf of that society, expa-•

tiated upon the advantages secured to those identi-
fied with it, and narrated the numerous cases of
accidents which none could have foreseen, in
which provision had been made for their members
unfortunately disabled. Ile sketched, in a graphic
speech, the benefit resulting from membership
with their body, which offered such advantages
that no commercial undertaking could possibly
hold out; that Ithe machinery was simple and
economical, and was not expended in costly build-
ings, serious printing charges, nor heavy manage-
ment expenses.

Messrs. Austin, Carke, Lindsay, Macdonald,
Taggart, and others, having addressed the meet-
ing, the proceedings terminated with the Usual
vote of thanks to the chairman.

TH.t MABTRIt 8110EMAKETtS.

At a meeting of muster shoemakers, held at the
Co.operative Hall, Downing-street, on Wednesday
night, it was resolved that a society should be
formed, and named "The Master Shoemakers'
Trade Protection Society." One hundred members
were enrolled. A committee was appoin,ted, with
officers, and Mr. Griffis addressed the meeting upon
the present advance in wages and material, which,
he said, amounted in the former from 20 to 25 per
cent., and the latter 15 per cent., within the last
twelve months; and he argued that unless they
became organised, and adopted a more uniform rate
of prices, the workmen would ultimately be in a
better position than the employers. He suggested
that a statement be drawn out for the regulation
of the trade, and for public guidance, to be placed
in the shop of each employer. It was ultimately
agreed to leaie the committee to draw out a state
-
merit of prices, to be submitted at the next general
meeting.

TILE AMALGAMATED WOOD TURNERS.

On Saturday last, ,a large conference of the
above society was held in Manchester, at which
upwards of 60 delegates of all the branches of the
wood-turning trade, from London, 13irmingham,
Manchester, Leeds, Exeter, Belfast, Preston,
Leicester, Mansfield, Wellington, Sheffield, Glas-
gow, Blackburn, and all the principal towns 'in the
Northern, Midland, and Western counties, were
present.
The business commenced at ton a.m., Mr.
W. Newton, of Leicester, being unanimously elected
to the chair.

The Chairman, in his opening remarks, said it
gave him great pleasure to preside over so large
and influential a number of representatives. On
no previous occasion during the seven years the
society had been established had the trade been
so thoroughly represented. Ire was happy to con-
gratulate them on the fact that the society had
increased by upwards of one thousand members
during the past year, and that members were join-
ing from all parts of the country. Ire believed
the increase next year would more than double
their numbers.

Mr. Ogden, the permanent secretary, reported
that the majority of the members of the society
had received an advance on their wages of from
10 to 16 per cont., and that this advance had been
gained with very little opposition on the part of
the employers, as the strike pay only amounted to
£2166e. 3d., and for funeral and emigration pur-
poses, £33; management expenses, £3B 10s. 2d.;
which loft the finances in a very flourishing
condition.
After the adoption of the report, several im-
portant questions affecting the general interest of
this trade were submitted to the conference, which,
after thorough and calm consideration, were un-
animously adopted.
It was decided to hold the next conference at
Manchester.

MISCELLANEOUS TRADES NEWS.

SHEFFIELD. - Over 200 MEtBOl29 in Sheffield
struck work on Saturday morning for 401 hours.
The Sheffield bricklayers' strike has terminated,
the masters having acceded to the men's demands.
The Atlas, the Cyclops, and one or two other
large works in Sheffield arc threatened with stop-
page on account of the notion of the boilermakers.
It is the practice to repair the boilers at these
establishments during the Whitsuntide and other
holidays, and this week the boilernutkers went to
make their usual inspection and to effect repairs.
The fitters got hold•of them, and persuaded them
to demand double time, and because their request
was refused they struck work. The machinery
cannot start until their work is completed.
Nuwny.--Three hundred dressers have struck

an advance of 30., and their employers will give
no more than 2s.

PUESTON.—A meeting of the master carpenters
of Preston has boon held, to consider the applica-
tion of the men for shorter hours. After a short
discussion, it was resolved to reduce the working
hours five hours a week.

COUNWALL.—Tho movement for obtaining in-
creased wages and reduced hours of labour is being
actively carried on in Cornwall. The members of
the Truro Police Force have each been granted an
advance of 2s. per week, and the ,satne amount
bae beeit granted to the junior wQrupken. in the

extensive foundry at Hayle. At Bedmin a com-

and neighbourhood with a view to the adoption of

HAWICK.—Two-thirds of the operative masons
in Hawick have struck, the masters refusing to
reduce the hours from 57 to 61 per week, though

FAILSWORTIL—On Wednesday "night a public
meeting was held at the Pole-lane School, Fails-

resist a proposed reduction in the prices paid for

do the same. There was a unanimous feeling for

DUNI:MR.—The Dundee journeymen bakers met

articles.text:
CONFERENCE OF IRONWORKERS.

A. conference of ironworkers was held at Shef-
field on Monday and Tuesday. The number of
men represented was between 40,000 and 60,000,
employed in Staffordshire,
,East Worcestershire,
Gloucestershire, Monmouthshire, Scotland, and
elsewhere. Mr. Ancott presided.

The object of the conference was to endeavour
to unito the whole of the ironworkers in the
United Kingdom in one national association, so
that the some policy might. be pursued by all. As
the prices of iron rise and fall in the different
markets simultaneously, so it is thought should
wages rise and fall at one and the same time
throughout tho whole of the iron districts.
The following resolutions were adopted
"That there shall be one national union extending
to all ironworking districts and embracing all
ironworkers, including blast furnacemen and
others connected with the trade who are disposed
to associate with us." "That to enable the iron-
workers to accomplish the above object the dele-
gates assembled at this conference agree, in the
name of their constituents, to accept and abide by
the revised rules which have received the careful
cOnsideration of Dir. Rupert Kettle, with such bye-
• laws as may be agreed to by the delegates assem-
bled, and which in their opinion are desirable to
promote efficiency in the working department of
the association. All bye-laws to be approved by
at least three-fourths of the members before they
become binding." It having been agreed. that
2,000 members should have the privilege of
appointing an age.nt, the following resolution was
passed :—" That there shall be an agent appointed
from Staffordshire and East Worcestershire, as
soon as the recognized number of members,
according to the monthly. return from the above-
named districts amounto to 2,000."
It was arranged that delegates should be sent
out as soon as possible to the various districts,
where there is no association of ironworkers, with
the object of getting the men to unite. The con-
terence, which had sat with closed doors, concluded
about six o'clock.
