articles.title: AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF ENGINEERS.
articles.text:
AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF
ENGINEERS.

Mr. William Allan, the zealous and able
,seere-
tary of the Amigamated Society of Engineers,
in issuing the twenty-first annual report of the
society, says :

"Fellow Members,—ln submitting the twenty-
first annual report of our society, I feel a Pleasure
in once more addressing you on the prosperous
condition of the trade generally, as well as on our
financial position. It has unfortunately been ray
lot for several years (with the exception of 1870)
to announce a yearly decrease in our accumulated
fund; but on the present occasion, I am pleased to
state, that during the past year we have added no
less a sum than £33,858 12s. 71-d. to our previous
balance, so that on the last meeting night in
December, 1871, our total balance amounted to
£116,326 6s. 7id.

"The year 1871 has proved not only exceed-
ingly prosperous, financially speaking, but has
also proved the most eventfnl one in the history
of trade societies, for by our compact organisation
we have effectually secured an important reduction
in the hours of labour, not only in the iron trade
but in many other branches of industry, and,
having obtained such an important boon, it is
hoped the artisans will take every advantage of
the change to promote the welfare of themselves
and families.

"While referring to 1871, I cannot let it pass
without alluding to the Criminal Amendment Act,
an act which was quite uncalled for, indeed only
intended to operate in the interests of capital, and
to prevent, if possible, workmen from maintaining
their rights and privileges; we must, therefore,
never rest until this disgraceful Act is totally

repealed.
"During the past year, I am happy to say, our
progress in establishing new branches and increas-
ing our members has been moat satisfactory, ten
new branches having been opened, six in the
United States, namely—Schenectady, Brooklyn,
Providence, Louisville, Cleveland, and Port
Huron; one at Forfar, in Scotland, and three in
England, namely—Durham, Wellingborough, and
Paddington, London; and during the same period
4,714 new members were admitted, BO that at the
close of the year we had 336 branches, with
37,790 members.

"For the year I find the total income amounted
to £91,271 9a. 3d., to which must be added
£82,467 6s. 110., that being the balance at the
end of December, 1870, making a total of
£173,738 16s. 30., and the expenditure during
the year having amounted to £57,412 9s. Bd., left
an accumulated balance of £116,326 6s. 70. to

the society's credit, a result which must be highly
gratifying, considering the drain upon the funds in
the previous years of depression.
"The amount paid as donation benefit to our
unemployed members (including £142 4s. sd.
as contingent benefit) has amounted to
£12,357 17s. 9d., or £20,349 19s. 7d. lo is than
was paid in 1870. For sick benefit we have
expended £18,496 4s. 2d., being £3OO Bs. 4d. in
excess of the amount paid in 1870, In seven
cases of accident we have paid £lOO to each, giving
a total of £7OO.
"The payments made to our superannuated
members show an aggregate of £8,942 6s. 3d.,
being a few pounds less than in 187 Q. On the
present, m on other occasions, I cannot refrain
from drawing the attention of the members to
the sums annually expended in support of this
benefit, more particularly since the last delegate
meeting, which took place in 1864. In referring
to the subject I have no wish or desire whatever
to cause any unpleasantness, but on the contrary,
simply to point out that at, no distant day the
whole question will undoubtedly have to be dealt
with, and arrangements made in respect thereto

of a more permanent character; indeed, when I
find the amount paid as superannuation during the
year under review Las been about two-thirds the
sum required for donation, and about one-half the
amount paid as sick benefit, I consider it my
bounden duty to claim attention to the subject, so
that when the fitting time arrives it may receive
that due consideration which its importance
demands."

articles.text:
AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF
RAILWAY SERVANTS.

Sr. PANCRAB.—A meeting will be held on
Sunday next, May 26th, at 6.30 p.m., at the
George the Fourth Tavern, Willes Road, Kentish
Town, for the purpose of forming a branch of the
Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants, to be
called the Midland or St. Pancras Branch. The
objects of the Society will be fully explained by
Dr. J. B. Langley, LL.D., or Mr. Geo. Chapman,
General Secretary pro tern, and other members of
the executive council. It is hoped that all classes
of the Midland Railway servants will come for-
ward at this meeting and join the Society, and
show the public that the men are like the masters,
not behind ether companies in looking after their
own interest. The chair will be taken at 7 o'clock
precisely. _

ALDGATE.—An important meeting of railway
servants was holden Friday last at tho Green Man,
Somerset-street, Aldgate. A gentleman highly
valued and much respected by those who know
him, occupied the chair, and in a very telling
speech explained the objects of the meeting,
forcibly impressing on his hearers the advisability
of unity and protecting themselves from the
unjust and harsh treatment so often experienced
by many. Ile alluded to the fact that the institu-
tion was not only acknowledged by the travelling
public but the press had supported them in
endeavouring to obtain concessions fair and just.
The Chairman read extracts from the BEE-HIVE
—(cheers)—and the leading article in the Deptford
arotaiele, and was frequently interrupted by
applause. Mr. Chapman followed and addressed
the meeting at great length. The name of Dr.
Langley, chairman of the Executive Council, was
greeted with deafening cheers, all present standing,
and a most enthusiastic scene prevailed, the cheer-
ing being repeated several times and continuing
for some minutes. It was unanimously agreed to
establish a branch, and a good list of names was
furnished. The principal offteers of the branch
were unanimously elected, each pledging his best
efforts to the cause, and it was resolved that in the
event of any man being " SPOTTED " that a levy
be made to support him. (Cheers.) Votes of
thanks were given to Dr. Baxter Langley, Mr.
Bass, M.P., Mr. Geo. Chapman, and the Chairman,
accompanied with much cheering, and the meeting,
was adjourned till Sunday, the 6th Arno at 6.30
p.m., when it is hoped Dr. Langley will be able to
attend and deliver an address.

BERMONDSITICo...A. crowded meeting of railway
mew was held on Sunday at the "Old Rose,"
Russell-street, Bermondsey, after the appointment
of a chairman and vice-chairman, Dr. Langley
was called on to address the meeting, which he did
at some considerable length, pointing out the
advantages of unity, he commented at great
length on the good feeling existing among all
classes, and concluded a most excellent address by
inviting all to join the "Amalgamated Society."
Mr. Geo. Chapman next addressed the meeting,
and explained the objects of the society, together
with the benefits conferred on those who became
members. It was resolved to open a branch of the
society. A well filled list was handed to the general
secretary, and the greatest unanimity prevailed.
Votes of thanks to Dr. Langley, C. Whitby, Esq.,
banker, Mr. Geo. Chapman, and the Chairman,
closed the laboure of the evening. The meeting
stands adjourned for Sunday, June 2nd.
SOUTH EASTERN Bwrcn.—A special meeting
was held at the Winchester Arms on Saturday
night last, the vice-chairman of the Branch
occupying the chair. The room was much
crowded. After the enrolment of a considerable
number of new members and other business, the
chairman said that they were in the proud posi-
tion of being eble to elect the delegates to the con-
ference in June, and they had met that night to
nominate them with a view to their election at the
next meeting. The nomination was accordingly
made. Some discussion then arose on the general
conduct of the subordinate ofileials, who had a
bonus on the reduction of expenses, and the system
was denounced as impolitic, because it assumed
that the official would not perform his duty
unless stimulated by a bribe, whilst, on the
other hand, the bonus tended to sacrifice
public safety to false economy. Dr. Baxter
Langley then addressed the meeting, and
in an earnest appeal to the audience, impressed
upon them the duty especially paramount at the
present moment of so conducting all their proceed-
ings as to show their employers that they were
not unreasonable or vindictive, and to prove to
the public that the cause of the railway servants was
the interest and safety of those who travelled along
the lines. lie counselled prudence in language,
caution in act, and faith in each other. They
were on the eve of a great meow, which never-
heless required the utmost care to beoure, and the

opportunity might be lost by dissensions on the
one hand, or rashness on the other. He looked
forward to the delegate meeting in June with the
deepest solicitude and anxiety, and hoped thatthat
deliberative assembly would be guided to wise and
prudent resolutions, because their decisions would
be fraught with important consequences not only
to the railway men of the time, but to their
children's children. Votes of thanks concluded
the proceedings.
STnoon.—On Friday last, Dr. Baxter Langley
and Mr. George Chapman attended by invitation a
meeting of the railway servants of Rochester,
Chatham, and Strood. The room was incon-
veniently crowded. Mr. Chapman was called to
the chair, and addressed the meeting at consider-
able length, being again and again interrupted by
applause. Ho called upon Dr. Baxter Langley to
address the meeting. A scene of great enthusiasm
prevailed at the conclusion of his speech, which
occupied three-quarters of an hour. A branch
was at once formed and some of the officers
appointed, another meeting having been fixed for
an early date. Votes of thanks were given to the
deputation who were escorted by friends to the
railway station, also to Mr. W. Bass, and the Editor
of the BEE-HivE. The business of enrolling
members occupied the officers till a late hour.
CAnnirr BIiANCIL-A very largo mating of
railway servants was hold at this place on Sunday
last, several travelling many miles to attend and
take part in the duties of the evening, and to
assist in the good cause so much to be valued by
all classes thoroughout the land. Those present
were singularly fortunate in having such a gentle-
man as the chairman to preside over them, for he
wont into business in such a spirited manner as to
prove he was no stranger to matters of such great
and deep importance. Ninety members were
announced, and it was stated that the branch will
be over 300 strong before the 21st of June next.
The officers were then appointed, and a well-tri;icl
and trusty servant nominated as the representa-
tive for the "ensuing delegate meeting." Votes
of thanks to Mr. Bass, M.P., the vice-presidents,
Dr. Langley and Mr. Goo. Chapman were given,
end one of the best and most enthusiastic meetings
over held in this part of the country was brought
to a close by a cordial vote of thanks being given
the chairman, who, amidst immense cheers, de-
clared the meeting adjourned to Sunday next,
May 26th, and to meet at the same hour as men-
tioneti on the notices.

STRATIPO (Essax) BRAN cm—Tho regulai
meeting of this branch was held on Saturday last,
at the "Commercial Hotel," Martin-street; the
members mustered in very strong force. The
Secretary road the minutes of the previous meet-
ing, which were unanimously confirmed. Several
names were added to the roll, which now number
nearly 300 members. Many very important
matters were considered, and a thorough good
understanding among all seemed to exist, for every
resolution was carried with acclamation as follows:
—" That a special general meeting of this branch
be convened at this house on Sunday, May 26th,
or on Sunday, June 2nd, to suit the convenience
of the members who desire to subscribe to the
levy for the 'Delegate Expense Fund ; ' and that
Dr. Baxter Langley be earnestly requested to
attend and take the chair," A vote of thanks was

then given to Dr. Langley and Mr. George Chap-
man, after which the meeting separated.
PADDINGTOII.--.A. l'lrgo number of railway em-
ployes assembled at the "Red Lion," Paddington,
on Friday last. The chair was taken by a yery
energetic railway man. A branch was formed,
officers elected, and over 50 names added to the
number already on the books. The usual vote of
thanks to the chairman closed the meeting. It now
stands adjourned till Friday next.

At Bow-street, further evidence has been
taken in support of the charges of burglary
against a police-constable of the E division,
his wife, and mother.in-law. There are
several cases against these persons, and the
allegation of the prosecution is that they not
only stole valuable documents from certain
chambers in Gray's Inn, but afterwards
endeavoured to obtain the reward offered for
their recovery. The prisoners who reserved
their defence were committed for trial.
A namßny deserving some considerable attention
among all classes of the 'community has of late
obtained great popularity, both in this country and.
abroad; we allude to .ahurses Goldin Lotion for
eruptions of the skin. The success of this pre-
paration is said to be most unusually great, as
many cures of skin diseases, and of wounds and
ulcers, are known to have taken place in a few
days, when other means of cure have totally failed.
It is claimed for this preparation that its discovery
was made upon a scientific basis' after years of
study and experience in the various forms of disease
for whiok it is designiad. It is quite certain that
sailors value it gieatly for scurvy, and in conse-
quence of its general utility we are induced to call
attention to it in these columns as an article which
should at least be known by every householder.

articles.title: COAL MINERS.
articles.text:
THE COAL MINERS.

MEETING AT MARYIIILL.

On Thursday forenoon, the 16th inst., a mass
meeting of the miners of the above-named
district was held to consider the Amended Truck
Bill and other matters connected with the welfare
of the men of the district. Mr. John Bowie
presided.
Mr. M•Donald, president of the Miners National
Association, at considerable length explained the
nature of the amendments on the Payment of
Wages Bill. Beheld it now to teem with clauses
that would lead to all kinds of truck pure and
villanous.

On the close of the address, the following re-
solution was moved by Mr. Samuel Hughes,
seconded by Mr. M‘Phie, and carried with great
acclamations of applause:—
" That the miners of Maryhill, who long
antlered from truck, saw with pleasure early this
session that the Right Hon. 11. A. Bruce in-
troduced the Payment of Wages Bill. We now
learn with regret bow much the Bill has been
altered; ve earnestly pray the Homo Secretary to i
introduce amendments n committee that will bring
back all the true features of the original Bill."
It was next agreed that the resolution be sent
to the Home Secretary, signed by a delegate from
each mine in the district. It was after this
agreed by ballot to obtain an advance. A hearty
vote of thanks was given to the speakers at!the
close of the meeting.

MASS MEETING IN TUE GLASGOW DISTRICT.

On Friday evening a mass meeting of all the
miners on the north side of the Glasgow district
was held near Tolleross, when Mr. ll'Donald, after
detailing the position of the Mines Bill, the ono
for Arbitration, and the Bill for Compensation for
Accidents, proceeded to discuss the merits of the
Government Bill, and pointed out the faults of the
measure as amended by the Select Committee. At
the close of the address it was moved by one of the
workmen, and agreed to unanimously, that the
meeting send a memorial to the Right Hon. It
Bruce, asking him respectfully to restore the Bill.
to its original form by amendments in committee.
It was next agreed that the memorial be signed by
a representative from each colliery tl that effect.
A motion was thereafter made that Monday, the
3rd of June, be a general holiday, that all the
men there present might go to Stirling to meet
the miners of Fife, Claekmannan,
Baillieston, and all others that may attend there
that day.

articles.title: IfiBB MEETING AT DAILLIESTON.
articles.text:
IfiBB MEETING AT DAILLIESTON.

On Thursday a mass meeting of the miners of the
Daillieston district was held to consider tho Masters
and Servants Bill. The whole of the men of the
district, which number fully 1,800, were idle to
attend the meeting. Mr. Scobie presided, and
introduced Mr. M`Donald, who proceeded to
explain the Bill as issued by the Government, and
ordered to be print ad by the House of Commons
on the 22nd of February, 1872, after which he
reviewed the Bill that had been presented to the
House as the work of the Select Committee. He
again maintained that it was a bill to promote
truck. not to destroy it. The following resolution
was put and unanimously agreed to :—" That this
meeting hail with pleasure the introduction of the
Bill by Mr. Henry A. Brace, entitled the Payment
of Wages Bill. They find in it real remedy for
truck. They now regret deeply to learn the Bill
has been all but destroyed by a Select Committee.
In all the circumstances they would most earnestly
entreat Mr. Bruce to bring forward such amend-
ments to the Bill when it goes into committee as
will restore it to its original form." It was
further decided to send the resolution to Mr.
Bruce. The usual complimentary votes concluded
the proceedings.

articles.title: TILE COLLIERS' STRIKE AT SEMIAM.
articles.text:
TILE COLLIERS' STRIKE AT SEMIAM.

On Monday the miners of Seaham and Seaton
Collieries resumed work on the terms against
which they struck on Monday week. This result
has been brought about by the meeting of dele-
gates in the city of Durham on Saturday, which
has been anticipated so anxiously by the men. At
this meeting the ease of the Seaham men was
taken up by the delegates, and a long discussion
ensued. Ultimately two motions were proposed,
one that the men should give a fortnight's notice,
and resume the strike at the end of that time; and
another that the. matter be submitted to arbitra-
tion. On a division the latter was carried by a
majority of 109 votes. On Sunday morning a
meeting of the miners was held at the colliery,
and, after the result of the delegate meeting had
been heard, it was resolved to accept it as satis-
factory. A deputation was at once appointed to
wait upon the viewers, who agreed that the men
should return to work.

DEMONSTRATION OF MINERS AT DARLASTON.

A denionstxation of South Staffordshire mine's
was made Qn Monday at Datia,ton, Between oliOlt

and nine thousand miners assembled at the fair
wake, at mid-day, and, forming into a procession,
walked through the streets of the town. A large
display of banners and flags, supplemented by the
strains of six or seven brass bands, made the pro-
cession unusually exciting to the many inhabitants
who crowded the streets to witness it. After the
procession a mass meeting was held, Dr. Cropp in
the chair, at which the following resolutions were
passed

Mr. Robert Edge (Wednesfield) moved the fol-
lowing resolution : —" That this meeting tenders
its thanks to the colliery and ironstone. mine pro-
prietors of South Staffordshire for of late conceding
the great reduction of the hours of labour, and
giving an equal or proportionate rice in the pick-
men's wages; and hopes that the
_peaceable and
satisfactory relations which now exist between
the employers and their workmen may long con-
tinue; and considering the mutual arrrangements
made hitherto on various
.questions, leads us to
hope that in future strikes and lock-outs will be
avoided by resorting to reason rather than the
arbitrament of war."

Mr. 'Walter Westwood (Wednesfleld) seconded
mo'io-y.

Mr. Wm. Drowa (delegate from the Amalga-
mated Association of Noah Staffordshire Miners)
supporta. the resolution, which was carried un-
animously.
Mr: G. Carter'(Darlaston) proposed the second
resolution :—" That this meeting believes that
union amongst miners is a necessity in the
amelioratien of their condition, and expresses
its pleasure in seeing union spreading again
among the miners of South Staffordshire. We
further express our entire confidence in the Amal-
gamated Association of Miners, and consider every
miner who does not join the same is neglecting a
duty hnowes to himself and to his family, iseeing
that the.ol;joets 'sought to be obtained are Calcu-
lated to benefit the mining population both
physically, sea:illy, morally,nnd,intellectually."._

- Mr. Joseph Harper (Brownhills) seconded the
motion, which-, after being supported by Mr. G.
Pickard (miners' agent, Cannock Chase), wn3
enthusiastically carried.
Mr. John Jones (Willenhall), moved a third
resolution expressive of satisfaction with the
Governtnent Mines Regulation Bill, and thanking
her Majesty's Ministers for bringing the measure
forward; expressing a hope, however, that the
Bill would not be injured in its passage through
the House, and protesting against the mutilation
of the Wages Bill by the Select Committee, aithe
amendments by that committee were calculated, if
adopted by the 'House, to legalise truck in its
worst form. It was, therefore, hoped Parliament
would refuse to adopt the Bill, a pledge being
given that the miners would do all in their po'wer
to resist the measure until the same was re•amended
seas to ensure weekly payments without any
deductions.

Mr. Enoch Onions (Willenhall) seconded the

motiou.

Mr. Halliday (President of the Amalgamated
Association) supported it, and it Was adopted
unanimously.

articles.title: LONDON 00ACHMAICERS AND THE NINE HOURS MOVEMENT.
articles.text:
THE LONDON 00ACHMAICERS AND
THE NINE HOURS MOVEMENT.

On Friday night an aggregate mooting of the
operatives engaged in the various branches of tho
coaclunaking trade of London was held at St,
James's-hall, in furtherance of the Nine Hours
Movement. The large hall was crowded to MOBS.
The Earl of Shaftesbury had been announced to
preside, but having to leave town auddenly, ho
sent a letter of apology, in which be wished every
success to the Nino Hours Movement.

In the absence or his lordship, Mr. Frankum
the chairman of the Coachmakers' Nine Hours
League, occupied the chair.
Mr. Brown, the secretary, then detailed tho
circumstances which had led to the formation of
the league and the calling of the present meeting.
He also read letters from Mr. S. Morley, M.P.,
Mr. P. H. Taylor, M.P., Mr. T. Hughes, M.P.,
Professor Fawcett, M.P, and other gentlemen,
cordially approving of the movement.

The Chairman then briefly addressed the meet-
ing, and said the movement was receiving the
support not only of the society, but of the non-
society men, and it only required united action to
obtain the object of the meeting.
Mr. Asplin then moved the following resolu-
tion:—" That in the opinion of this meeting it is
desirable that the working hours in the coach
trade in London, should ho reduced to 54 per
week, a boon which is now enjoyed by almost
every trade in the United Kingdom.,,
Mr. Bonner seconded the resolution, which was
earned unanimously.

Mr. Rearmly moved the following resolution :
" That this meeting desireu tho oummittoo of tho

London United Coachmakers' Nine Hours League,
to draw up a memorial to be presented to the
employers, praying for the adoption of those hours,
*ith a regudst that a reply bo giten on or before
this day Month; and that the mdvement become
general from the Ist of July next."
Mr. R. Lander seconded the resolution, which
was also carried.

Mr. Hills then moved—" That in the opinion of
this meeting it is desirable that the arrangement
of OA hours be left to the employer and the men
iii eaoh establishment, with the one exception that
the shops be universally closed at one o'clock on
Saturdays."
Ilk. Castelld seconded the resolution, whioh wds
agreed to. A resolution was also adopted upon
the motion of Mr. Balcomb, seconded by Mr.
Read, pledging the meeting to support the league
in all its movements to gain the object in view.

tliE AGITATION OV talli LONDON

CARPENTERS.

On Saturday night last a crowded meeting of
delegates from the carpenters and joiners in the
Vaiiotni tendon building firms was held at the
Brown Bear, Bloomsbury, for the purpose of
deciding upon the firms where the men shall be
called out oa the Ist of Juno next, in accordancq
with the resolutions adopted at the aggregate
meeting of, the trade in St. James's-hall, on Tues-
day night last. Mr, Sadler occupied the chair.
A report was brought up from the Nine Hours
Committee on the present pdsition of the move-
Merit, and rebordmetelitig the ndliieS o seveial
firms for the delegates to decide upon two out of
the number, when action should be taken on
Saturday, the let of June, unless in the meantime
some overtures were received from the Masters'
Assdoiatidn. After adnsiderable discussion; it was
fesolved that the Workmen in the employ of
Messrs. Jackson and Shaw, of Pimlico, and
Messrs. Brass, of Old-street, St. Luke's, should
Wait, by deputation, upon their respective
employersi and inform them that they should
leave their employ on Saturday, June 1, unless
they complied with the terms contained in the
men's memorial. The delegates from those firms
stated it as their opinion that the decision of the
Meeting would be promptly complied with.
The remainder of the business transacted was of
A financial character, with the exception of the
appointment of a deputation to be in readiness to
meet the employers, if so re ci nested.
The action taken by the operatives from time to
time becomes loofa td the public from the fact
that reporters are not excluded from their meet,
itigs, but no reporters are allowed to be present at
the meetings of the assodiated employers forming
the Master Builders' Association, *hick are held
at the Freemasons' Tavern, and therefore it•is
difficult to ascertain the results of their discus-
alone. It it stated, however, that a Meeting of
.the Associated Masters lute been held sine° the
meeting of the men in St. James's-hall, and that
after discussion it was resolved to meet the with-
drawal of the men from any particular firm or
firms by a general lock-out so far as the firms con-
ne3ted with the Association were concerned. It is
also stated that this decision was far from being
unanimous, and that many of the members wore
in favour of a compromise by meeting the
demands of the men for 151 hours per week at 9d,
per hour with a counter-proposition for 61 hours
at 80. per hour, which would be a • reduction of
2i hours on the present working week, and one
halfpenny advance in the rate of wages per hour.
Beth masters and men are preparing for the
coming struggle.

A. Special Correspondent, with the Living-
stone Search Expedition, writing from Zanzi-
bar on the 19th of April says that up to that
date no letters had been received either from
Dr. Livingstone or Mr. Stanley, the American.
War was still going on in the interior, and if
affairs continued unsettled when the Expedition
approached the disturbed districts a detour
would be made to the southward to avoid the
contending parties. The hurricane which oc-
curred at Zanzibar on the 15th ult. did im-
mense damage, and the Abydos the only
vessel which escaped, saved herself by steam-
ing at full speed with two anchors ahead.
There was considerable loss of life. Two
millions, it is estimated, will barely cover the
,direct damage to property, and European
residents expect that a famine may be the re-
sult.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL
articles.text:
THE AGRICULTURAL

LABOURERS.

LONDON CENTRAL AID COMMITTEE.—At a meet- •
ing of tile Agricultural Ldhourers London Central
Aid Committee, held at the tact SWan, liyder's-
court, Leicester-square, on Saturday night, air..
Smith, in the chair, who said that he considered
this movement of the agricultural labourers one of
the greatest social questions that has arisen for
many years. The Secretary, Mr. Canharn, said
hehad received a letter from Cambridgeshire, stating
there was a strike at a village called Bottisham,
about seven miles from the town of Camtiridge,
where the men were getting eleven shillings per
week, they lidve asked for a shilling rise to make '
their wages equal to the wdges thtit dre paid in the
neighbouring villages, which is on the aVerage
about twelve shillings per week. He also said
there was a strike in• Dorset, at a village called
Melbourne St. Andrews, the men were getting
nine shillings per week, and now they demand a
rise of three shillings, and a reduction of one hour
in eech week. Mr. Murray moved that the sum
of three pounds be sent to Melbourne St. Andrews,
Dorset, to aid the agricultural labourers, who are
on strike and in great distress. Seconded by Mr.
Bailey, and carried, •
WILTSHIRE,—On Friday eVening a meeting of
agricultural labourers was held on Lyueham-
green ; Lord Edmund Fitzmaurice, M.P., pre-
siding. The meeting was called in connection
with the West of England Agricultural Labourers'
Association, with the view of forming a branch
society. The evening proved to be most wretched
and miserable ae fegards the weather, there being
scarcely any cessation in the rain, which began to
fall early in the day and continued until lato in the
evening; yet there wore about 800 labouring
men and women assembled under the wide-
spreading branches of the large elm tree where
the meeting was held at 7 o'clock. A serious
grievance of the agricultural labourers was
,touebed upon -- the limitations upol which
they hold their cottages. In most cases the
cottages are held by the tenant farmers who are
apt to turn a man out at a week's notice when ho
is ne longer employed upon the farm. Thomas
Fry told a stdry of a landlottra steward, the truth
of which was corroborated by Lord Edmoed
Pitzunaurico, who said he had made a thorough
inquiry into its correctness. This man Fry said:
-ee" He didn't blame landlords so much as their
stewards. Some years ago a poor widow went to
the steward to pay her rent, when the steward
axed her where her two sons were working, and
she told him that one was working for Mr. So-
and-so, and the other was working at the Swindon
factory, when the steward told her that, unless
her on left Swindon factory' and came back to
work for a farmer, she was to be turned out of her
cottage," This regard for tho fortunes of the
widow and the fatherless was unjustly attributed
to the agent of Lord Edmond' brother, the
Marquis of Lansdowne, one of the most excellent
and liberal-minded landlords in the country.
Lord Edmond's investigations proved that the
threat was delivered by the agent of a clergyman!
KENT.—On Monday evening last two large
gatherings of agricultural labourers of the western
parts of the county of Kent were hold, the first
on the Brent, near Dartford, and the other at the
Royal Oak, Northumberland-green, near Erith,
for the purpose of discussing their grievances and
organising branches in co-operation with the
Agricultural Labourers' Union, recently esta-
blished at Maidstone. The weather being fine
and the day being. a holyday, the attendance was
very numerous. at both places, and there was a
manifest determination to join earnestly in the
agitation for increase of wages and reduction of.
he hours of labour. Mr. Simmons, of Maid-

stone, and others connected with the move-
ment addressed the meetings. Arrangements
were made for the formation of branches
of the union at Dartford and Erith, and
the proceedings terminated. The agitation in
Suffolk is not diminishing. Those on strike make
it a practice to parade the streets with a view of
exciting sympathy. Those in the vicinity of
Chedburgh and Depden have struck for an advance
to 135., and refuse to take 12s. Employers have
in salllty instances expressed a willingness to give
the 135., but the men will not rest satisfied until
they get 155., and this the employers cannot afford
to give. The agitation is causing a stagnation in
agricultural pursuits, but masters will not give in
tO unreasonable demands.
OXFORDEMIRE.—During the week several largo
and enthusiastic open-air meetings have been held
in North Warwickshire, and in and near Danbury
in Oxfordshire, and about a dozen branches of the
union formed. The Warwickshire Union has now
50 branches and nearly 6,000 members. A party
of labourers left Banbury for Brazil last week,

and next week a farmer at Napton, Warm ickshire,
takes out 60 men to the same country.

Yonx. —On Saturday, at the York Corn
Exchange, Mr. O'Brien, ILA., delivered a lecture
on agricultural strikes, their origin and cure, com-
bined with the contrast of town, country, and
foteign labour, Mr. G. A. Dean, of London, pre-
sided. Mr. O'Brien said he was there to over-
throw the teaching of violent professed dema-
gogues. Ho then showed that strikes were good
for the unskilful and indolent, but ruinous to the
industrious and skilful, and traced their origin to
a debased literature, to a gross materialism, and to
the doctrines on the land question taught by Mr.
Bright and Mr. it S. Mill. He regretted the
position of the agricultutal labotrer in Dorset and
Devon, but offered his congratulations that the
farm labourers in Yorkshire were well paid and
well cared for. He asked them to pause before
they broke up the ties which had for ages bound
tho employer and labourer together in friendship
and good feeling, and to remember that the
English farmer was, with open ports,:e9ntending
against the closed ports of the world, lie pointed
out the remedies to be applied, which he based
upon an improved system of education, sanitary
laws, and cherishing a good feeling between the
governing and governed classes.
KIRKCALDY.—The agricultural labourers in the
neighbourhood of Kirkcaldy resolved on Saturday
night to agitate for shorter hours and increased
wages.

Lord Brownlow has adranced his labourers'
wages to 16s. 6d. per week, and reduced their
hours by half an hour daily, and they are to
cease work at three o'clock on Saturdays.

HunuronnsuritE.—A mass meeting of agricul-
tural labourers took place at Harewood End, be-
tween Hereford and Monmouth, on Thursday
night. There was also a number of farmers and
farmers' sons present. Mr. Gibson Ward, of
Herefordshire, and Mr. Strange, of Shropshire,
were present. Several labourers told touch-
ing tales of misery, and from their statements

10s. a week seemed to be the general wage. The
meeting was very stormy, and a fight--which
commenced between the farmers and their labourers
—was stopped by the police. Mr. Gibson Ward
announced that in case it should be found neces-
sary to strike substantial support had been pro-
mised from Birmingham and Leamington, and
Lord Fitzmaurice and the Hon. Auberon Herbert
had promised to make a ten days' sojourn in the
county, holding meetings each evening. Mr.
Strange announced the formation of a Hereford-
shire union, which demanded for the men 14s.
a week in winter, and 16s. a week in summer, wet
or dry, otherwise 3s. a day. A largo number of
labourers joined the union. The farmers after-
wards held a conference, aud some thirty or forty
were said to be prepared to give 168. a week, with-
out perquisites.
HAmaarro's.—On Monday afternoon Canon
Girdlestone gave a, farewell address to a large
number of agricultural labourers at Ilalberton.
' The Canon, who was frequently applauded, said:
—" On first coming to Halberton ho was astonished
and depressed at the poverty of the agricultural
labourers in this district. For years he had been
sending labourers to Yorkshire and other northern
parts of England; he had sent away four hundred
from that parish and neighbourhood, and thirty
more were about to go, leaving behind them 9s.
a week in Devonshire for 188., 198., and 295. in
Yorkshire. He hoped there had been a cor-
responding benefit to the labourers left behind.
Some good had been accompli,shed, if he had
been rightly informed that within the last few
months the farmers bad given an increase of ls.
per week. He strongly urged the labourers to be
united, and pointed out the benefit of unions."

The Master and Servant (Wages) Bill has been
examined and amended in Select Committee. The
Bill now extends to Ireland. Some alteration has
been made in the clause relating to weekly PP'
ment of wages; wages are to accrue due weekly
(or at less intervals if so agreed) and are to be
paid within a week after the end of
the week which they accrue duo (or 41i
lees intervals if so agreed) ; but the contract
may specially provide for the payment at that time
of a part not being less than 75 por cent., and the
residue within a week of the balance being struck
on the completion of the work. The Bill is not to
render invalid contracts for deduction from wage'
of money advanced by the master to the workman,
or rent of premises let to him; or of a stun io
respect of medical attendance, medicine, or sub'
seription to an infirmary, or dispensary, or ill
respect of fuel for domestic use, or of ma'
terials, tools, OT implements (other than
gas or steam power) supplied by the
master for use by the workman in his work, or
of provender supplied for consumption by ,en
animal employed by the workman in his work, or
in respect of victuals dressed or prepared under the
roof of a master and there consumed by the work-
man, so that. tho sum deducted for fuel, materials,
tools, implements, provender, or victuals do not
exceed their real and true value; but no deductio,
is to be made in respect of medical attendance
when the majority of the workmen shall have
notified in writing their objection to the medical
attendant employed. The Bill is not to authorhe
any deduction from wages in respect of the use or
standing of any stocking frame or machine. There
is to be a penalty of 10s. a day for using such
frame or machine in the manufacture of any
articles for persons other than the master. The
Bill is not to prevent payment of wages at
the place of ordinary employment, although
contiguous to a house licensed for sale of intoxi-
cating liquors or at a shop, provided the master
has no interest in the trade. So far as concerns
the prohibition of payment of wages in drink, and
conditions as to spending wages in drink, and
deductions or actions in respectof drink, the Bill
is to extend to workmen in husbandry. The power
of the Secretary of State to grant exemption with
respect to the time of payment of wages, or to
certain deductions from *ages, is to extend to
cases where it is shown that by reason of the
workman incurring or sharing the risk of profit or
loss, or the difficulty of ascertaining the wages
earned within the periods limited by the Bill, or
by reason of other exigencies in particular cases,
it is expedient to grant such exemption. The.
penalty for offences against this Act is not to
exceed £lO for the first, £5O for the second, £lOO
for a subsequent offence. In paying wages, bank
notes current in the place are to be deemed coin
of the realm. The Bill, as amended, has been
re-printed.

Thn judge who was appointed to the Kansas
district court by Mr. Lincoln is accused of
conducting his court in a rather free and
easy way, especially when under the influence
of liquor. When in this condition he is re-
ported to have told a convicted prisoner that

would sentence him to only three pars, and
give him a letter of introduction to the
warden of the prison, whom he knew very
well, and who, he was sure, would treat him

reception. The Flying Squadron, under the

boat that conveyed him on shore. According

India seemed much pleased with the loyal and
hearty reception accorded to him by all classes.
Its imposing nature is even said to have taken -
him somewhat aback. In the evening be was
present at a ball given at Government Hone e
to the dicers of the Flying Squadron, and on
the day of the departure of the mail he was to
unveil the statue of Queen Victoria, presented
to the city by the late Guicowar of Baroda.

rarliament, rendered vacant by the death of

districts, and the inhabitants forcibly removed

articles.title: HORSEWHIPPING A LABOURER.
articles.text:
HORSEWHIPPING A LABOURER.

A great meeting of labourers was held at
Bloxham, near Banbury, the other evening.
Mr. Mooney, one of the speakers, said that a
most scandalous affair had occurred at Tad-
marton, where Mr. Charles Garrett, a far-
mer, had accused a labourer named Bodfish,
of making the men dissatisfied with their
condition, and of having attended a 'union
meeting. While Bodfish was at work in a
field Mr. Garrett went up to him, told him he
had come to give him a good thrashing, and
then began belabouring him with his riding
whip, continuing to do so until he was quite
exhausted. The man on the following day
went to the superintendent of the County
Police at Banbury, who referred him to the
magistrates' clerk, who sent him with a note
to Mr. Norris, a magistrate for the county,
living at Swaleliffe, near where the ft,satilt
was committed. Mr. Norris read the
note, and asked Bodfish if he wanted a sum-
mons, to which he replied he did. Mr. Norris
said that before he could grant the summons
he must see Mr. Garrett. (Laughter, and a
voice, " That's justice.") Mr. Norris told him
to o2me back again next day, and he did so.
Mr. Norris then told him that he had seen
Mr. Garrett, and said that it was a very
serious affair; he hoped, however, that Bod-
fish felt disposed to settle the matter. If he
pressed the law a summons must be granted,
but he would. not have one penny recompense,
and would only get his law expenses. Mr.
Norris said he would give £3 to settle it, but
Bodfish refused to take it, and as he was leav-
ing the house Mr. Norris called him back and
offered him £1 more, saying that it would be
to his advantage to take the money. Mr.
Norris afterwards admitted to Bodfish that he
had done wrong, but that he did it for peace
and quietness. The speaker added that no
magistrate would have interfered had It been
the case of a poor man, and Mr. Norris had
exceeded his duty as a magistrate, and that
he must be disqualified from acting any longer
as such.

articles.title: REPUBLICANISM IN NEWCASTLE.
articles.text:
REPUBLICANISM IN NEWCASTLE.

A conference of the members of the Northern
Republican League was held on Monday after-
noon, in the Club Room, Pilgrim-street, New-
castle—Mr. James Birkett, president, in the
chair, when various matters concerning the
Republican movement in this district- were
brought under consideration.
Mr. Brodie, of North Shields, advocated the
desirability of Republicans directing their
attention to securing the election of repro.
eentatives •holding their own views on &hod
Board, on Town Councils, and in Parliament.
Mr. O'Hanlon, of Newcastle, delivered an
address on Republican propagandism.
Mr. Bay&ld spoke on the question of
Parliamentary representation, and advised the
appointment of sub-committees who should
devote themselves to such details as looking
after the registration, the votes given by
Members of Parliament, and other business.
Mr. Cresswell complained .of the circum-
stance that Bills were frequently smuggled
through Parliament without the attention of
the public being called to their nature.
Mr. Barry denounced the Illegal Assemblies
Act.

Votes of thanks were accorded to Mr.
°Manion, Mr. Bayfield, and the chairman,
and the meeting adjourned.
A tea, concert, and ball took place in the
evening, under the auspices of the Newcastle
and Gateshead Republican Club.

At Whitwick, Leicestershire, a working
man having lost a child, the officiating clergy-
man refused to bury it on the ground that it
had not been baptised. There being no other
burial ground available, and interment in the
nearest cemetery being too expensive, a funeral
service was conducted in the public street at
eight o'clock in the evening. A considerable
number of persons attended to show their
sympathy with the bereaved parents.
